subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: In the beginning there was only Ginnungagap, the yawning void, with fire-world Muspelheim to the south and ice-world Niflheim to the north. Where their heat and rime met, the frost dripped into life and the primal giant Ymir took shape. From his slain body the gods Odin, Vili, and Ve fashioned the earth: his flesh the soil, his blood the seas, his skull the dome of the sky. Through all the nine worlds stretched Yggdrasil, the great ash whose roots a serpent gnawed and whose branches an eagle crowned.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: Beneath one root of Yggdrasil lay the Well of Urd, where the three Norns drew water each day to keep the tree from rotting. Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld carved the fates of gods and men into the trunk, and not even Odin could unwrite what they had inscribed. The squirrel Ratatoskr scurried up and down the bark, carrying spiteful messages between the eagle in the crown and the dragon Nidhogg coiled among the roots, so that the World Tree was never truly at peace.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: The first man and woman, Ask and Embla, were shaped from two driftwood logs the gods found upon the shore. Odin gave them breath, Hoenir gave them sense and motion, and Lodur gave them warmth and the bloom of living color. Lifeless wood became thinking flesh, and from this pair every human generation descended, walking the middle realm of Midgard that the gods had ringed with the eyelashes of Ymir to keep the giants out.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: Odin hungered for wisdom above all things, and so he hung himself upon Yggdrasil for nine windswept nights, pierced by his own spear, an offering of himself to himself. He neither ate nor drank, and at the ninth dawn he glimpsed the runes shimmering in the well below and seized them screaming. Knowledge always demanded a price in the north, and the All-Father paid it again at Mimir's well, surrendering one eye for a single draught of its waters.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: The dwarves were not crafted with care but bred like maggots in the dead flesh of Ymir, and the gods, finding them clever, gave them shape and reason. Four of their kind, named Nordri, Sudri, Austri, and Vestri, were set at the corners of the world to hold up the great bowl of the sky. They became master smiths, forging Thor's hammer, Odin's spear, and the golden hair of Sif from threads spun in their lightless halls.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: Day and night were not abstractions to the Norse but a pursuit across the sky. The maiden Sol drove the sun's chariot and her brother Mani steered the moon, each fleeing forever before a ravening wolf. When at last the wolves caught them at Ragnarok, the heavens would darken and the stars would fall. Until then the chase explained every dawn: the light running, the dark hunger close behind, and the brief mercy of the day between.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: The rainbow bridge Bifrost arched from Midgard to Asgard, a span of fire, air, and water that only the gods and the worthy dead could cross. Heimdall kept its gate, needing less sleep than a bird and able to hear grass growing in the meadows and wool lengthening on the sheep. His horn Gjallarhorn lay ready, and on the day it sounded across the nine worlds, every god would know that the final battle had begun and the bright bridge would shatter under the weight of the giants' march.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: Yggdrasil was destined to survive even Ragnarok. When fire and flood had swallowed the old world and the gods lay dead in the ash, a man and a woman named Lif and Lifthrasir would emerge from their shelter within the tree's trunk, having fed on the morning dew through the long catastrophe. From them a new humankind would spread across a green and risen earth, proof that the World Tree was not merely a structure but the deathless thread of the cosmos itself.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: Among the roots of Yggdrasil dwelt the well of Hvergelmir, the seething cauldron from which all rivers flowed. There the dragon Nidhogg gnawed without pause at the tree's deepest fibre, and around it writhed so many serpents that no tongue could number them. The Norse imagined the cosmos as a living thing under constant attack, kept upright only by the labor of the Norns, so that existence itself was an act of stubborn, daily repair.

subtopic: Norse creation and the World Tree
sentence: The giant Ymir was not the only being to wake in the dripping void. The primeval cow Audhumla appeared beside him, and from her udders flowed four rivers of milk that nourished the giant. She herself licked the salty rime-stones for sustenance, and over three days uncovered a buried figure, Buri, the grandfather of the gods. Thus the first nourishment of the world came from a cow, and the first ancestor of Odin was freed by the patient work of her tongue.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles slew his own children, and to cleanse the stain the Oracle bound him to serve King Eurystheus for twelve labors. The first sent him against the Nemean Lion, whose pelt no weapon could pierce. Heracles cornered the beast in its double-mouthed cave, blocked one exit, and strangled it with his bare arms. Afterward he skinned the lion using its own razor claw, and ever after wore the impenetrable hide as a cloak that no spear could bite.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: The Lernaean Hydra was a horror of many heads, and for each one Heracles smashed, two more sprouted hissing from the stump. Realizing brute force only multiplied his enemy, he called his nephew Iolaus to sear each severed neck with a burning torch. The last head was immortal, so Heracles buried it still snapping beneath a great boulder. He dipped his arrows in the monster's venomous blood, a poison so potent it would one day, by a long and cruel chain of fate, bring about his own death.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: To clean the stables of King Augeas, where three thousand cattle had fouled the ground for thirty years, Heracles refused the obvious labor of the shovel. Instead he tore open two walls and rerouted the rivers Alpheus and Peneus straight through the filth, flushing decades of dung away in a single day. Augeas, having promised a tenth of his herd as payment, refused once the work was done, and so Heracles later returned with an army and killed the faithless king.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: The eleventh labor demanded the golden apples of the Hesperides, guarded by nymphs and a hundred-headed dragon at the edge of the world. Heracles sought out the Titan Atlas, who held the sky upon his shoulders, and offered to bear the burden himself if Atlas would fetch the apples from his own daughters. Atlas agreed, but on returning he meant to leave the hero stooped forever. Heracles, feigning agreement, asked only that Atlas hold the sky a moment so he could pad his shoulders, then snatched the apples and walked free.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: For the final labor, Heracles descended into the underworld to bring back Cerberus, the three-headed hound that guarded the gates of the dead. Hades granted him the beast on one condition: that he subdue it using no weapon at all. Heracles seized the dog by its straining throats, endured the bite of its serpent tail, and hauled it living into the sunlight, where the very sight of it turned Eurystheus white with terror. The labor done, he carried Cerberus gently back to its post.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: The Ceryneian Hind was sacred to Artemis, a deer with golden antlers and bronze hooves that could outrun an arrow. Eurystheus chose it precisely because harming it would offend the goddess. Heracles pursued the creature for a full year across mountains and rivers, never wounding it, until at last he caught it sleeping. As he carried it home, Artemis confronted him in fury, but he pleaded necessity, blamed Eurystheus for the command, and was permitted to complete the labor unpunished.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: The Stymphalian birds infested a dark marsh, their feathers sharp as arrows and their droppings poisonous to crops. Heracles could not wade into the bog to reach them, so Athena gave him a pair of bronze krotala forged by Hephaestus. He clashed the rattles together, and the birds, panicked by the unbearable din, burst from the reeds in a screaming cloud. As they wheeled overhead, the hero shot them down one by one, and the survivors fled the marsh forever.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: The death of Heracles came not in battle but through love and old poison. The centaur Nessus, dying from one of the hero's hydra-tipped arrows, told Heracles's wife Deianira that his blood was a charm to secure a husband's faithfulness. Years later, fearing a rival, she soaked a tunic in the centaur's gore and sent it to her husband. The venom seared his flesh beyond bearing, and Heracles built his own pyre upon Mount Oeta, climbed upon it, and was carried in flame to join the gods.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: To capture the Cretan Bull, the very beast that had fathered the Minotaur, Heracles travelled to the island and wrestled it into submission with his bare hands. He shipped it back across the sea to Eurystheus, who dedicated it to Hera. The goddess, refusing any gift that glorified her hated stepson, drove the bull away. It wandered to the plain of Marathon, where it terrorized the countryside until the hero Theseus, a generation later, came to finish what Heracles had begun.

subtopic: Greek labors and the hero Heracles
sentence: The mares of Diomedes were beautiful and terrible, kept by the Thracian king and fed on the flesh of unwary guests. Heracles overpowered the grooms, drove the man-eating horses to the shore, and when Diomedes pursued with his soldiers, the hero fed the king himself to his own beasts. Sated on the flesh of their master, the mares grew calm at last, and Heracles led the now-docile horses back to Eurystheus, who set them loose on the slopes of Olympus.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The kitsune is the fox spirit of Japanese folklore, and the older it grows the more tails it sprouts, until at nine hundred years it possesses nine and shines with a golden or white coat. A kitsune can take human form, most often a beautiful woman, to deceive or to repay a kindness. Stories tell of fox-wives who lived happily with mortal husbands for years, bore them children, and vanished only when a barking dog or a careless word revealed the tail they could never fully hide.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The kappa haunts rivers and ponds, a green child-sized creature with a beaked face, a turtle's shell, and a shallow dish of water set into the crown of its head. Its strength depends entirely on that water, and a clever traveler facing a kappa need only bow politely; the courteous creature bows in return, spilling the precious dish and rendering itself helpless. Kappa relish cucumbers and the livers of the drowned, and parents long warned their children away from deep water by invoking the lurking river-imp.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The tengu were once feared as malevolent demons of the mountains, long-nosed or bird-beaked beings that abducted children and led monks astray. Over centuries their reputation softened, and they became guardians of remote peaks, masters of swordsmanship who tested and sometimes trained worthy warriors. The legendary swordsman Minamoto no Yoshitsune was said to have learned his uncanny blade-skill from the tengu of Mount Kurama, dancing through the dark trees with feathered teachers no human eye could follow.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: A tsukumogami is an ordinary household object that has reached its hundredth birthday and, on that anniversary, awakens into a living spirit. A discarded paper lantern grows a single eye and a lolling tongue; a worn umbrella hops about on one leg; a tea kettle sprouts the head and tail of a badger. The belief carried a quiet moral, urging people to treat their tools and possessions with respect, lest a lifetime of neglect return to them as a resentful, animated thing.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The yuki-onna, the snow woman, appears to travelers caught in blizzards as a tall pale figure in a white kimono, beautiful and unbearably cold. With a single breath she can freeze a man to death, or she may simply lead him deeper into the storm. In one famous tale she spares a young woodcutter on the condition that he never speak of their meeting, then years later reveals herself as his own wife, dissolving into mist the moment he breaks his promise.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The rokurokubi seems an ordinary woman by day, but in the dark hours her neck stretches to impossible lengths, drifting through the house like a serpent while her body sleeps undisturbed. Some rokurokubi are unaware of their own nature; others use the affliction to spy, to frighten, or to lap at lamp oil. The horror of the legend lies less in malice than in concealment, the unsettling thought that the quiet person beside you harbors a secret that uncoils only when you are not looking.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The oni are the brutal ogres of Japanese myth, towering creatures with red or blue skin, wild hair, and horns, often clutching a spiked iron club called a kanabo. They burst from the gates of hell to punish the wicked and devour the unwary. Yet the festival of Setsubun turns the tables each year, when families fling roasted soybeans through their homes shouting that demons must leave and good fortune enter, driving the oni out with nothing more fearsome than a handful of beans.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The noppera-bo is a faceless ghost, and its terror is purely psychological. It first appears as an ordinary person, perhaps a kind stranger who stops to ask why a traveler is weeping. Then it raises a hand and wipes its features smooth, leaving a blank expanse of skin where eyes and mouth should be. The traveler flees in horror to a lamplit shop, gasping out the tale, only for the shopkeeper to ask, did the face look something like this, and slowly erase its own.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The tanuki, a real raccoon dog elevated into a mischievous folk spirit, is a shapeshifter famous for transforming leaves into counterfeit money and for tricking gullible merchants. Unlike the cunning and sometimes dangerous kitsune, the tanuki is bumbling and good-humored, a creature of comic appetite and harmless deceit. Statues of the round-bellied tanuki, hat tilted and sake flask in hand, still stand outside Japanese restaurants, inviting customers in with a folkloric promise of prosperity.

subtopic: Japanese yokai and supernatural beings
sentence: The onryo is the vengeful ghost, almost always a woman wronged in life, who returns from death in a white burial robe with long black hair hanging loose over a pale face. Her grief and rage are so absolute that they spill outward, cursing not only those who harmed her but anyone who crosses her path. The tale of Oiwa, betrayed and poisoned by her husband, made the onryo the enduring template of the Japanese ghost story, the dead returning not for justice alone but to spread their suffering.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: When an Egyptian died, the soul began a perilous voyage through the Duat, the underworld, toward the Hall of Two Truths. There the heart of the deceased was placed upon a great scale and weighed against the feather of Maat, the goddess of cosmic order and truth. Anubis steadied the balance while Thoth recorded the verdict. If the heart, heavy with sin, sank lower than the feather, the monster Ammit, part lion, part hippopotamus, part crocodile, devoured it, and the soul was destroyed forever.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: Osiris, the green-skinned king of the dead, had once ruled Egypt as a living god until his jealous brother Set tricked him into a beautiful coffin, sealed it shut, and cast it into the Nile. His wife Isis recovered the body, but Set found it again and tore it into fourteen pieces scattered across the land. Isis gathered every fragment, bound them with linen, and with her magic breathed enough life into Osiris for him to father a son, Horus, before descending to rule the underworld.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: Each night the sun god Ra sailed his solar barque through the twelve hours of the underworld, and each night he faced the same enemy. The colossal serpent Apophis, embodiment of chaos, lay in wait to swallow the sun and end the world. The gods of the dead and the souls of the righteous took up spears to defend the barque, and Set himself, for all his treachery, stood at the prow to drive his blade into the serpent. Every sunrise was a victory wrested from the dark.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: The Book of the Dead was not a single scripture but a collection of spells, illustrations, and instructions written on papyrus and buried with the dead to guide them through the Duat. Among its passages was the Negative Confession, in which the soul stood before forty-two divine judges and denied each sin in turn: I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not caused tears, I have not stopped the flow of water. To pass, the deceased had to know the name of every gate and every guardian.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: Isis was the great enchantress of the Egyptian pantheon, and a famous tale tells how she gained power over even Ra himself. Knowing that a god's true name held the source of his strength, she fashioned a venomous serpent from the dust mixed with the sun god's own spittle. The creature bit Ra, and as the aged god burned with poison, Isis offered to heal him only if he whispered his secret name. In agony he yielded it, and the goddess became the equal of the sun.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: Horus, son of Osiris and Isis, grew to manhood determined to avenge his father and reclaim the throne from his uncle Set. Their struggle lasted eighty years, fought as battles, contests, and trials before the council of the gods. In one clash Set tore out the eye of Horus, but the wounded eye was healed by Thoth and became the wedjat, the symbol of protection, restoration, and royal power. In the end the gods awarded the living world to Horus and the desert to Set.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: The Egyptians believed a person was made of several distinct parts that death scattered and the funeral rites had to reunite. The ka was the life-force that required offerings of food and drink; the ba was the personality, depicted as a human-headed bird that could fly from the tomb by day; the akh was the transfigured spirit that joined the eternal stars. Only when ka, ba, and the preserved body were properly tended could the dead achieve a lasting and blessed existence.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: The goddess Nut arched her star-spangled body across the heavens, her fingertips touching one horizon and her toes the other, while her brother and husband Geb lay beneath as the rolling earth. Each evening Nut swallowed the sun, and through the night it travelled the length of her body, to be born again from between her thighs at dawn. The air god Shu held her aloft, keeping sky and earth eternally apart so that the world might have room to exist between them.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: The Field of Reeds, called Aaru, was the Egyptian paradise that awaited souls who passed the weighing of the heart. It was imagined as an idealized mirror of the Nile valley, with fertile fields, abundant harvests, and the company of loved ones who had died before. Yet even paradise required labor, and so the tombs were stocked with small carved figures called shabti, servants who would answer in the owner's place if the gods called upon the dead to till the eternal soil.

subtopic: Egyptian gods and the afterlife journey
sentence: When the goddess Sekhmet, the lion-headed bringer of plague, was sent by Ra to punish humanity, her bloodlust grew so terrible that she threatened to wipe out every living person. Ra repented and devised a trick: he ordered vast quantities of beer dyed red as blood and poured it across the fields. Sekhmet, mistaking it for the gore she craved, drank until she fell into a deep and peaceful sleep, and when she woke her rage had cooled into the gentler form of Hathor.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Long ago all the stories in the world belonged to the sky god Nyame, and there were no tales for people to tell. Anansi the spider climbed to the sky and asked to buy them, and Nyame, amused, set an impossible price: the spider must capture the python that swallows men whole, the leopard with terrible teeth, the hornets that sting like fire, and the unseen fairy who fears no enemy. Anansi, small and clever, accepted, and by his cunning won them all.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: To catch Onini the python, Anansi cut a long bamboo pole and walked through the forest arguing loudly with his wife, though she was not there. He declared aloud that the python was longer than the pole, then that it was shorter, until Onini, vain and curious, asked what the fuss was about. Anansi offered to settle the matter by measuring, and the python, eager to prove its great length, allowed itself to be stretched along the pole and bound fast.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Anansi once tried to hoard all the wisdom in the world inside a great clay pot, planning to hide it high in a tree where none could reach. He tied the pot to his belly and began to climb, but the bulging vessel kept slipping and blocking his way. His young son, watching below, called up that it would be far easier to carry the pot on his back. Hearing this, Anansi realized that not even he could gather all wisdom, and in his frustration he flung the pot down, and the wisdom scattered across the whole earth.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: To capture the leopard Osebo, Anansi dug a deep pit along the path the great cat used at night and covered it with branches. When Osebo tumbled in, the spider appeared at the rim and pretended to pity him, offering to help. He lowered sticky webs and bent a young tree over the pit, then tricked the leopard into tying himself to it. The tree sprang upright, leaving Osebo dangling helplessly, and Anansi carried his second prize up to the waiting sky god.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Anansi heard of a magnificent feast and resolved to eat at every cooking pot in the village without missing a single one. He spun eight long threads, tied one end of each around his waist, and gave the other ends to eight people, instructing each to tug when the food was ready. But every pot finished at once, and all eight strands pulled at the same moment in eight directions. The threads cinched tight, squeezing the spider's once-broad body into the narrow, pinched shape it has worn ever since.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: The fairy Mmoatia was the hardest of Nyame's four prizes, for she was a creature no one could see. Anansi carved a small wooden doll, coated it with sticky gum, and set a bowl of mashed yams in its lap beside a forest path. When the fairy came and the doll did not answer her polite greeting, she struck it in anger and her hand stuck fast. She struck again with the other hand, then kicked, until she was caught entirely, glued to the silent doll by her own temper.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Anansi was famous for his bottomless greed, and one tale tells how he wished to keep an entire pot of beans for himself rather than share it with his family. He hid the hot pot under his cap, claiming he had simply taken a vow of silence and could not eat. The beans steamed and scalded his scalp, and when he could bear it no longer he tore the cap away. The boiling beans had cooked every hair from his head, and that, the storytellers say, is why the spider is bald to this day.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: When the great famine came, Anansi sent his son Kweku Tsin to search for food, and the boy found a magic stone that, when struck and addressed politely, would summon a feast. Anansi, learning the secret, hurried to use the stone himself, but in his impatience he forgot the necessary words and the order of the ritual. The angry spirit of the stone gave him nothing, and the trickster, for once outwitted by his own haste, went home as hungry as he had come.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: Anansi's stories travelled across the Atlantic in the memories of enslaved Africans and took new root in the Caribbean and the American South, where the spider became Aunt Nancy and slipped into the Br'er Rabbit tales. In bondage the trickster who survives by wit rather than strength carried a hidden meaning, a quiet assurance that the small and powerless could still outmaneuver the strong. The stories endured because they were never only entertainment.

subtopic: West African Anansi the spider trickster
sentence: In one tale Anansi grew jealous of his friend the chameleon, who owned a fine field of grain. The spider dug a covered tunnel into the field and stole the harvest, then mocked the chameleon for having nothing. But the chameleon, slow and patient, wove a coat sewn entirely with living vines and went to visit Anansi. As he walked the coat seeded the spider's path with sprouting greenery, and soon the whole village could trace the stolen grain straight back to the trickster's door.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: The Tuatha De Danann, the divine race of Irish myth, did not vanish when the mortal Milesians conquered Ireland. Instead they withdrew into the Otherworld, the realm beneath the green hills and ancient burial mounds called sidhe. From these earthen palaces they became the aos si, the fairy folk, neither gods nor ghosts but a separate people living alongside the human world, glimpsed at twilight and feared at the turning festivals of the year.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: Tir na nOg, the Land of the Young, lay across the western sea, a country where no one aged, no one sickened, and the trees bore fruit and blossom at once. The warrior-poet Oisin was carried there by the fairy woman Niamh of the Golden Hair and lived in joy for what seemed three years. When he longed to see Ireland again, Niamh warned him never to let his foot touch mortal soil, but a fall from his horse aged him three hundred years in an instant, for that was the true span he had been away.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: The banshee, from the Irish bean si meaning woman of the fairy mounds, was an omen of death attached to certain old families. Her keening wail, heard in the night around a household, foretold that one of its members would soon die. She might appear as a young woman, a stately matron, or a withered crone washing bloodstained linen at a ford. The cry was not a curse but a warning, the Otherworld giving notice that one of its own threads was about to be cut.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: At the festival of Samhain, the boundary between the human world and the Otherworld grew thin, and the sidhe rode abroad in great processions. Mortals left offerings of food and milk to placate the fairy host, and travelers feared being swept up by the Wild Hunt or led astray by lights dancing over the bog. The dead, too, could return on this night, and the living masked themselves so that no wandering spirit or fairy would recognize and claim them.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: The changeling was the dark heart of fairy belief, the fear that the sidhe would steal a healthy human infant from its cradle and leave one of their own in its place. The substitute, often a sickly or aged fairy, was said to be revealed by strange behavior, an uncanny appetite, or an old and knowing look in a baby's eyes. The folklore was a grim attempt to explain illness and failure to thrive, and it sometimes drove desperate parents to cruel tests against a child they no longer believed was theirs.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: To eat the food of the Otherworld was to bind oneself to it forever. Many tales warn of mortals who stumbled into a fairy feast, a hall blazing with light and music in the heart of a lonely hill, and accepted a single cup or a bite of bread. Those who ate could never fully return to the human world; they wandered home decades later untouched by age, or never came home at all. The wise refused every offered dish, no matter how their hunger gnawed at them.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: The Dagda was a chieftain-god of the Tuatha De Danann, a vast and earthy figure who carried a club so heavy it rode upon wheels, one end of which slew with a blow and the other end of which restored life. He owned a magic cauldron that never emptied, feeding any host that gathered, and a great harp that, when he summoned it, flew through the air to his hand and could compel the seasons themselves to turn with its music.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: Iron was the great defense against the sidhe, who could not abide its touch. A nail driven into a doorframe, a horseshoe hung above the threshold, or an iron blade laid in a cradle would keep the fairy folk at bay. A midwife might place a poker across a newborn's basket; a traveler might carry a scrap of iron in a pocket. The belief reflected an older world giving way to a newer one, the fairies of the green age unable to endure the metal of the smith.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: Time ran differently in the Otherworld, and this was the cruelest of its enchantments. A man who spent what felt like a single evening dancing in a fairy ring might return to find his cottage gone, his family long dead, and his name a half-remembered story. Others vanished for a year and a day, the traditional span of fairy captivity, and came back unchanged while the world had moved on without them. The sidhe did not always mean harm; their gift of timelessness was simply not made for mortal lives.

subtopic: Celtic Otherworld and the sidhe
sentence: The leprechaun belongs to a humbler corner of Irish fairy lore, a solitary shoemaker of the sidhe, often heard before he is seen by the tap of his hammer on a single tiny shoe. He is said to guard a crock of gold, and any mortal quick enough to seize him can demand its location. But the leprechaun is a master of misdirection, and the foolish captor who glances away for even an instant will find his prisoner gone and his treasure no nearer than before.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: The gods, grown weary of the noise and tumult of humankind, resolved to wipe out the world with a great flood. But the wise god Ea could not bear the secret, and so he whispered it to a reed wall behind which the man Utnapishtim slept. Through the reeds the warning came: tear down your house and build a boat, abandon your possessions and save your life, take aboard the seed of every living thing. Utnapishtim obeyed, and the deluge that followed lasted six days and nights.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, was two parts god and one part man, and in his arrogance he oppressed his own people until they cried out to the heavens. The gods answered by creating Enkidu, a wild man who lived among the beasts, to be his match and his counterweight. The two fought a tremendous battle in the streets of Uruk, and finding neither could defeat the other, they embraced as friends, and the great adventures of the king truly began.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Gilgamesh and Enkidu journeyed to the Cedar Forest to slay its guardian, the monstrous Humbaba, whose roar was the flood and whose breath was fire. With the favor of the sun god Shamash, who sent thirteen winds to pin the monster down, they overcame him. Humbaba begged for his life, but Enkidu urged the killing blow, and they felled the great cedars and brought the timber home. That defiance of a divine guardian would later be counted against them by the gods.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: When Enkidu fell sick and died, condemned by the gods for the slaying of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, Gilgamesh was shattered by a grief he had never known. He would not allow the body to be buried until a worm crawled from its nose, and only then did he understand the finality of death. Terrified now for himself, the king cast off his royal garments, dressed in the skins of beasts, and wandered into the wilderness in search of the secret of eternal life.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Gilgamesh crossed the waters of death to reach Utnapishtim, the only mortal granted everlasting life, hoping to learn how he too might escape the grave. The flood survivor set him a simple test: to conquer death, first conquer sleep, and stay awake for six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh failed at once, slumbering where he sat, and a loaf of bread baked fresh each day was laid beside him to count his shame. He could not even master sleep, the small brother of death.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Out of pity, Utnapishtim told Gilgamesh of a thorny plant growing on the seabed that could restore lost youth. The king tied stones to his feet and sank to the depths, plucked the prickly plant, and rose triumphant, planning to share it with the elders of Uruk. But while he bathed in a cool pool, a serpent slid from the water and ate the plant, sloughing its skin as it went. The snake renewed itself, and Gilgamesh wept, for he had won immortality only to lose it to a passing snake.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: The goddess Inanna descended into the underworld to visit her sister Ereshkigal, queen of the dead. At each of the seven gates she was forced to surrender one ornament of her power, until she stood naked and powerless before the throne. The judges of the dead fixed her with the eye of death, and she was hung as a corpse upon a hook. Only the cunning of the god Enki, who fashioned two sexless beings to slip past the gatekeepers, won her release, and even then she had to find another to take her place.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: When Inanna returned from the underworld, demons clung to her, demanding the substitute the law required. She passed through her cities and found her servants in mourning for her, and would not give them up. But in Uruk she found her husband Dumuzi seated in splendor on his throne, untroubled by her absence. In her fury she set the demons upon him, and Dumuzi was dragged below, condemned to spend half of every year among the dead while his sister served the other half.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: The creation epic Enuma Elish told how the young storm god Marduk slew Tiamat, the vast salt-water dragon of primordial chaos. He drove the winds into her open mouth so she could not close it, then loosed an arrow that split her in two. From the upper half of her carcass he stretched out the heavens, and from the lower half he shaped the earth. Her weeping eyes became the sources of the Tigris and the Euphrates, and her ribs the arch of the sky.

subtopic: Mesopotamian flood and Gilgamesh
sentence: Gilgamesh returned to Uruk empty-handed, having found neither everlasting life nor the renewing plant. Yet as he approached the city, he gazed upon its mighty walls of fired brick, the orchards and the temple of Ishtar, and an old understanding came to him. He had built these walls; they would stand long after he was dust. The epic ends not with the conquest of death but with its acceptance, and with the quiet immortality of a great work left behind for those who come after.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: Vishnu, the great preserver, descends into the world whenever cosmic order falters, taking form as one of his ten avatars. The earliest were beasts and hybrids: Matsya the fish who towed the ark of humanity through a deluge, Kurma the tortoise who bore a mountain on his back, Varaha the boar who lifted the drowned earth from the cosmic ocean on his tusks. Each descent met a particular crisis, and together they trace a ladder of being rising toward fully human and finally divine kingship.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The fourth avatar, Narasimha, was born of a riddle. The demon king Hiranyakashipu had won a boon that no man or beast could kill him, neither indoors nor outdoors, neither by day nor by night, neither on the ground nor in the air. When he persecuted his own devout son Prahlada, Vishnu burst from a stone pillar at twilight as a being half lion and half man. On the threshold of a doorway, he drew the demon onto his lap and tore him apart with his claws, fulfilling every condition of the boon while violating none.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The dwarf Vamana, fifth avatar of Vishnu, approached the generous demon king Bali and humbly begged for as much land as he could cover in three strides. Bali, amused by the small request, agreed. Then Vamana swelled into a cosmic giant. With his first step he spanned the entire earth, with his second the heavens, and finding nowhere left for the third, the king offered his own head. Vishnu pressed Bali down into the underworld, but honored his devotion by granting him kingship there.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: In the Ramayana, the seventh avatar Rama, prince of Ayodhya, was exiled to the forest for fourteen years by the scheming of a jealous queen. There the demon king Ravana abducted his faithful wife Sita and carried her to the island fortress of Lanka. Rama, allied with the monkey army of Sugriva and the devoted Hanuman, built a bridge across the sea, waged a tremendous war, and slew the ten-headed Ravana, restoring righteousness to the world.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: Hanuman, the monkey-faced devotee of Rama, was a child of the wind god and possessed of immense and barely remembered power. To reach Lanka and find the captive Sita, he leaped across the entire ocean in a single bound. When Rama's brother Lakshmana lay dying, Hanuman flew to the Himalayas for a healing herb, and unable to identify the plant, simply uplifted the whole mountain and carried it through the air. He embodies selfless service, his strength awakened only in the cause of another.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: Krishna, the eighth avatar, is celebrated in countless tales of his playful childhood among the cowherds of Vrindavan. As an infant he was set upon by the demoness Putana, who tried to nurse him with poisoned milk, but Krishna drank her very life away. As a boy he stole butter, danced upon the hood of the serpent Kaliya to drive it from the river, and lifted the hill Govardhana on one finger like an umbrella, sheltering the village from a storm sent by an angry god.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: On the eve of the great battle of Kurukshetra in the Mahabharata, the warrior Arjuna surveyed the two armies and saw cousins, teachers, and elders arrayed against him. Despairing, he let his bow slip from his hands and refused to fight. His charioteer was Krishna, who then revealed his divine nature and spoke the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita, counseling Arjuna on duty, action without attachment, and the imperishable soul that no weapon can cleave.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The Mahabharata centers on a dynastic struggle between two sets of cousins, the five virtuous Pandavas and the hundred Kauravas. Through a rigged game of dice, the eldest Pandava gambled away his kingdom, his brothers, and even their shared wife Draupadi. The attempt to publicly disrobe Draupadi in the assembly hall was halted only by a miracle, as her sari lengthened endlessly, and this humiliation set in motion a war that would consume nearly every warrior of an age.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The tenth and final avatar, Kalki, has not yet appeared. He is prophesied to come at the close of the present dark age, the Kali Yuga, when righteousness has all but vanished from the earth. Riding a white horse and wielding a blazing sword, Kalki will destroy the wicked, end the corrupted age, and inaugurate a new cycle of cosmic order. Unlike the past descents that answered a single crisis, Kalki's coming will reset time itself, closing one great wheel of the ages and beginning another.

subtopic: Hindu epics and avatars of Vishnu
sentence: The churning of the ocean of milk was a vast cooperative labor between the gods and the demons, who together sought the nectar of immortality hidden in the depths. They used the mountain Mandara as a churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. As they pulled, the ocean yielded marvels and terrors alike: the wish-granting cow, the goddess Lakshmi, and a poison so deadly it threatened all creation, which the god Shiva drank and held forever in his throat, staining it blue.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The domovoi is the guardian spirit of the Slavic household, a small bearded man who dwells behind the stove or beneath the threshold. A well-treated domovoi protects the family, keeps the livestock healthy, and warns of coming trouble by moaning or rattling in the night. He demands respect and small offerings of bread and salt, and when a family moved house they would coax their domovoi to follow, carrying embers from the old hearth so the protective spirit would not be left behind.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: Baba Yaga is the fearsome witch of Slavic folklore, an old woman who lives deep in the forest in a hut that stands on enormous chicken legs and turns to face whoever approaches. Her fence is made of human bones topped with glowing skulls, and she flies not on a broom but in a great mortar, sweeping away her tracks with a pestle. She is neither wholly good nor wholly evil; she may devour the foolish, but she also tests and rewards the brave and the courteous who come seeking her aid.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The rusalka was the restless spirit of a young woman who had drowned, often one who died unbaptized or by her own hand after some betrayal. In early lore she lingered by rivers and lakes, and during the green festival of Rusalka Week she emerged to dance in the fields, bringing moisture to the crops. But her beauty was a lure, and a man who followed her into the water might be tickled to death or dragged down to drown in her cold embrace.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The leshy is the lord of the forest in Slavic belief, a shapeshifting spirit who can stand as tall as the highest pine or shrink to the size of a blade of grass. He herds the wild animals as a farmer herds cattle, and he delights in leading travelers astray, twisting paths into circles and imitating familiar voices among the trees. A lost wanderer who suspected the leshy's mischief was advised to turn every garment inside out and put the left shoe on the right foot, confounding the spirit's trick.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The vodyanoy was the malevolent water spirit of Slavic rivers and millponds, imagined as a bloated old man with a green beard, fish scales, and weeds tangled in his hair. He lurked beneath mill wheels and quiet pools, dragging swimmers and careless bathers to their deaths to swell the ranks of drowned souls who served him. Millers, whose livelihood depended on the water, treated him with wary respect and were rumored to offer him a black pig or a measure of grain to keep their wheels turning.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: Koschei the Deathless was the great villain of Russian wonder tales, a gaunt and cunning sorcerer who could not be slain by any ordinary means. His death was hidden away from his own body: it lay at the point of a needle, the needle in an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck within a hare, the hare locked in an iron chest, and the chest buried beneath a green oak on a distant island. Only a hero who unraveled this nested secret could finally bring the deathless one to his end.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The firebird of Slavic folktale is a creature of dazzling plumage, each feather glowing like a coal so that a single one can light a dark room. It is both a blessing and a curse to those who hunt it, for the quest to capture the firebird drives the hero of the tale into ever greater dangers. To merely glimpse the bird is to be seized by longing, and many a tsar's son set out after a fallen feather only to find that the prize, once won, demanded a still harder task.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The polevik was the spirit of the open field, who appeared at noon and could be deadly to anyone who slept in the furrows during harvest. A close kin was the poludnitsa, the Lady Midday, a woman in white who walked among the crops in the punishing heat of the day. She would question laborers with riddles, and those too dazed by the sun to answer might be struck with sickness or have their heads twisted around. The legend was a folk warning against working through the dangerous midday hours.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: The bannik haunted the Slavic bathhouse, a structure that stood apart from the home and was considered a place of both cleansing and danger. The spirit favored the third washing shift; anyone bathing too late risked being scalded, smothered with steam, or worse. To keep the bannik content, bathers left him water, soap, and a fresh birch besom, and they never bathed alone after dark. The bathhouse, where birth and divination once took place, was an uneasy threshold between the human world and the unseen.

subtopic: Slavic folk creatures and household spirits
sentence: Vasilisa the Beautiful, persecuted by her cruel stepmother, was sent into the forest to fetch fire from Baba Yaga herself, a journey meant to be her death. But Vasilisa carried a small wooden doll given to her by her dying mother, and when she fed it scraps of food it came alive to help her. The doll completed every impossible task the witch demanded, sorting grain and poppy seed through the night, until Baba Yaga, unsettled by the girl's hidden blessing, sent her safely home with a glowing skull.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: Maui was the smallest and youngest of his brothers, born premature and cast into the sea wrapped in his mother's hair, only to be rescued and raised by the gods. Though his family thought little of him, Maui grew into the great culture-hero of Polynesia, a demigod whose cleverness reshaped the world. His deeds were not the solemn acts of a creator but the bold, trickish exploits of an underdog who refused to accept the limits set for mortal beings.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: The islands of the Pacific were Maui's catch. Sailing far out with his brothers, he lowered a magic fishhook baited with blood from his own nose and felt a tremendous weight take hold. He chanted and strained until a great fish rose dripping from the depths, and that fish became the land. The North Island of New Zealand is still called Te Ika-a-Maui, the Fish of Maui, and the brothers' impatient hacking at it, before the proper rites were done, is why the island is rugged with mountains and valleys.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: In the beginning the days were too short, for the sun raced across the sky and people had no time to fish, to farm, or to cook their food. Maui resolved to slow it down. He plaited a great rope from the strong flax, snared the sun as it rose, and beat the blazing creature with the magic jawbone of his ancestor until it begged for mercy. The sun, battered and weary, agreed to crawl more slowly forever after, and that is why the days are long enough for the work of life.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: Humankind once shivered in the dark and ate raw food, for fire was hidden away. Maui set out to find it and came at last to the underworld home of Mahuika, the goddess of fire, who kept the flame in her glowing fingernails. She gave him fire freely, nail by nail, but Maui kept dousing each gift and returning for another, until the goddess in her fury hurled all her remaining fire across the land. Maui fled before the blaze, but the fire had soaked into certain trees, and from their wood people learned to draw it ever after.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: The greatest and last of Maui's deeds was his attempt to win immortality for all humankind by conquering death itself. The goddess of death, Hine-nui-te-po, slept with a body of stone and obsidian teeth between her thighs. Maui planned to crawl through her and emerge from her mouth, reversing the path of birth and so defeating mortality. He warned the birds who came with him to keep silent, but the little fantail, watching the demigod halfway inside the sleeping goddess, could not help laughing.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: The laughter of the fantail woke Hine-nui-te-po, and the goddess of death closed upon Maui and crushed the demigod between her thighs of stone. So the boldest of all the Polynesian heroes died in his last and most ambitious adventure, and because he failed, death remained the lot of every human being. The story does not mourn Maui's loss so much as accept it, explaining mortality as the price of a brave attempt rather than a punishment.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: In the Maori account of creation, the sky father Ranginui and the earth mother Papatuanuku lay locked in a tight embrace, and their children were crushed in the darkness between them. The children debated whether to kill their parents or to part them, and at last Tane, the god of forests, lay on his back and pushed with his powerful legs until sky and earth were forced apart. Light flooded into the world, but Ranginui's tears still fall as rain, and the mists rising from the ground are Papatuanuku sighing for her lost husband.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: Pele, the volcano goddess of Hawaiian tradition, journeyed across the Pacific in search of a home for her sacred fire. At each island she struck the ground with her digging stick, but her sister Namaka, goddess of the sea, pursued her and flooded every pit she dug. Only on the Big Island of Hawaii, in the deep crater of Kilauea, did Pele find ground high and far enough from the reach of the waves. There she dwells still, and the eruptions of the volcano are the goddess shaping the land that is hers.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: The demigod Maui is said to have stolen the secret of fishing nets, lifted the sky higher so people could stand upright, and given humanity countless other gifts through his restless cunning. Unlike gods who command from above, Maui worked from within the world, an outsider and a youngest child who proved his worth not by birthright but by daring. His tales spread across thousands of miles of ocean, varying island to island, yet always recognizably the story of the small one who would not be told what could not be done.

subtopic: Polynesian creation and the demigod Maui
sentence: Before Maui caught the islands, the great voyaging canoes had crossed the Pacific guided by the stars, and the navigators carried the names of their gods with them. Tangaroa ruled the ocean and all its fish, and a fisherman who set out without honoring him risked an empty net or a swamped canoe. The Polynesian myths braided together the practical knowledge of seafaring people with the deeds of their heroes, so that the same story might teach a child both how the world was made and how to read the swell of the waves.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: Among many peoples of the western plains and plateaus, Coyote was the great trickster, a figure of appetite and folly whose blunders often shaped the world. When the people first emerged into the land, it was Coyote who scattered the stars across the sky in careless handfuls instead of placing them in their proper patterns, which is why the heavens are sprinkled with disorder. He stole fire for humankind, but he also drowned, burned, and fooled himself a hundred times, dying and returning in tale after tale.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: In a story told among the peoples of the Pacific Northwest, the world lay in darkness because a selfish chief kept the sun, moon, and stars locked in carved boxes in his lodge. Raven, the trickster, transformed himself into a tiny hemlock needle, floated into the drinking water, and was swallowed by the chief's daughter, who gave birth to him as a child. Raven the infant cried and cried for the boxes until the doting grandfather opened them, and the trickster, seizing the light, became a bird again and flew it up into the sky.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: Iktomi, the spider trickster of the Lakota, was a being of clever speech and constant scheming who often outsmarted himself. In one tale he saw his own reflection in a still pond and, certain it was a rival hiding food, dove in again and again to fight the stranger, nearly drowning before he understood. The Lakota told Iktomi stories to teach by counterexample, letting children laugh at the spider's vanity and greed and learn, through his failures, what behavior the community would not abide.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: A widespread Coyote tale tells how the trickster, watching a flock of beautiful birds, begged to fly with them. The birds took pity and each gave him a feather, and Coyote rose into the air, drunk with joy and boasting that he flew better than any of them. Annoyed by his arrogance, the birds each plucked their feather back in mid-flight, and Coyote tumbled from the sky to the hard earth below. The story warns against pride and against accepting gifts only to mistreat the givers.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: The Anishinaabe tell of Nanabozho, a trickster and culture-hero born of a human mother and the West Wind. Nanabozho named the plants and animals, taught the people the use of medicines, and gave them the rites of the sweat lodge. Yet he was also a glutton and a fool, and many tales recount his ridiculous misadventures, for he could be both the wise teacher who shaped the world and the bumbling figure who got his head stuck in a moose skull and stumbled blindly into the river.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: Among several southeastern peoples, the rabbit was the trickster, small and weak but irrepressibly clever. In one famous tale Rabbit was caught and the angry animals debated his punishment, and Rabbit, feigning terror, begged them to do anything but throw him into the briar patch. Delighted to have found his weakness, they hurled him straight into the thorns, and Rabbit, who had been born and raised among the briars, called back his thanks and scampered away unharmed.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: A Coyote story explains the origin of death itself. When the first beings debated whether the dead should return, Coyote argued that they should stay gone, reasoning that the world would grow too crowded and that grief would soon be forgotten anyway. The others reluctantly agreed. But when Coyote's own child died, he was stricken with sorrow and rushed to bring the dead back, only to be told that the law he himself had made could not now be unmade. By his own clever argument, the trickster lost his child forever.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: Raven, on the northern coast, was forever hungry, and his greed drove the plot of many tales. In one, Raven tricked the sea-folk out of their store of fish, in another he stole a fisherman's catch by playing dead so convincingly that the man tossed his apparent carcass into the boat among the salmon. The trickster's appetite was bottomless, and though his schemes sometimes benefited the people, they were never undertaken for the people's sake; the world was simply shaped by the side effects of Raven feeding himself.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: The trickster of Native American tradition was never a simple villain. Coyote, Raven, Iktomi, and the others occupied a space between the sacred and the absurd, capable of creation and destruction in the same breath. They broke the rules so that listeners could see where the rules lay; they suffered the consequences of folly so that no one need suffer them in earnest. To tell a trickster tale was to teach without preaching, to bind a community together in shared laughter at a creature who was, in part, everyone.

subtopic: Native American trickster tales
sentence: In a Plains tale, Coyote grew envious of a friend who could throw his own eyes up into a tree to watch for game and call them back to their sockets. Coyote begged to learn the trick and was warned to do it no more than four times. He did it four times with delight, then once more in his pride, and his eyes lodged fast in the branches and would not return. Blind and stumbling, the trickster fashioned new eyes from pine pitch and berries, and that, the elders said, is why a coyote's eyes glow yellow in the dark.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: The boy Arthur did not know he was a king's son, raised in obscurity by Sir Ector after the wizard Merlin spirited the infant away. When the old king died leaving no acknowledged heir, a sword appeared thrust through a stone and anvil in a London churchyard, and upon it letters declared that whoever drew it forth was the rightful king of all England. Knight after knight strained and failed, until young Arthur, sent to fetch a blade for his foster-brother, pulled the sword free without even knowing the wonder of what he had done.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: The Round Table was given to Arthur as a wedding gift, and its perfect circle carried a deliberate meaning. At its rim no knight sat above another, for there was neither head nor foot to the table; king and humblest companion shared an equal place. The fellowship that gathered around it bound the knights to a code of mercy, courtesy, and the protection of the weak. One seat alone stood empty, the Siege Perilous, reserved for the knight pure enough to achieve the Grail, and fatal to any other who dared to sit in it.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: Excalibur was no common sword. When Arthur's first blade shattered in combat, Merlin led him to a still lake, and from its waters rose an arm clothed in white samite, holding aloft a gleaming sword. The Lady of the Lake granted Excalibur to the king, and Merlin counseled him that the scabbard was the greater gift, for while he wore it Arthur could not lose a drop of blood, no matter how grievous the wound. The treacherous theft of that scabbard would later cost the king dearly.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: Sir Gawain accepted the challenge of the Green Knight, a towering figure who rode into Camelot on a green horse and offered any knight a single blow of an axe, on the condition that he receive the same blow in a year and a day. Gawain struck off the giant's head, but the Green Knight calmly retrieved it and reminded Gawain of the bargain. The young knight's long journey to keep that terrible appointment became a searching test of his honesty and courage against the lure of survival.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: The quest for the Holy Grail drew the knights of the Round Table away from Camelot and ultimately hastened its end. The Grail, the vessel of the Last Supper, would reveal itself only to a knight of perfect purity, and most of Arthur's fellowship were found wanting. Lancelot, the greatest in arms, was barred by the sin of his love for the queen. It was Galahad, his son, conceived for this very destiny, who at last beheld the Grail uncovered and, his earthly purpose complete, was carried straight to heaven.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: The doom of Camelot lay coiled within its own splendor. Lancelot, the noblest knight of the Round Table, and Queen Guinevere fell into a love that honor could not sanction, and when their secret was at last dragged into the open, the fellowship split into warring factions. Arthur was forced to condemn his queen and make war upon his dearest friend, and while the king was abroad with his armies, his nephew Mordred seized the throne and the realm fell into ruin.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: The last battle was fought on the field of Camlann, where Arthur and the traitor Mordred met at the head of their broken armies. The king drove his spear through Mordred, but the dying usurper hauled himself up the shaft and dealt Arthur a mortal wound to the head. As the sun set on the slaughter, almost every knight of the Round Table lay dead, and the fellowship that had shone for a generation was extinguished in a single afternoon.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: Mortally wounded, Arthur commanded the surviving Sir Bedivere to cast Excalibur back into the lake. Twice the knight, unable to discard so great a treasure, hid the sword and lied to his king. Twice Arthur knew the lie. Only on the third command did Bedivere hurl the blade out over the water, and an arm rose to catch it, brandish it three times, and draw it under. Then a dark barge bore the dying king away across the mere toward the island of Avalon.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: Arthur was carried to the mysterious isle of Avalon, where, the legend insists, he did not die but only sleeps, his wounds tended by Morgan le Fay and her sisters. He waits there still, and in Britain's hour of greatest need he will return to take up his crown again. Upon his supposed tomb the words rex quondam rexque futurus were said to be inscribed: the once and future king. The hope of his return turned a tale of catastrophe into a promise that endured for centuries.

subtopic: Arthurian legend and the Round Table
sentence: Merlin, the prophet and enchanter who had set Arthur on the throne and guided his rise, did not see the fall of Camelot. The wizard fell hopelessly in love with the sorceress Nimue, sometimes called Viviane, and unwisely taught her every secret of his craft. When she had learned enough, she used his own spells to seal him forever within a tower of air, or a cleft oak, or a cave of crystal, depending on the telling. The wisest man in Britain was undone by the one thing his wisdom could not master.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: The Aztecs believed they lived in the age of the Fifth Sun, and that four worlds had been created and destroyed before it. The first sun was devoured by jaguars, the second swept away by hurricanes, the third consumed by a rain of fire, and the fourth drowned in a great flood that turned humankind into fish. Each destruction had reset the cosmos, and the current age too was destined to end, this time torn apart by earthquakes, a knowledge that gave Aztec religion its restless urgency.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: To bring the Fifth Sun into being, the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan and built a great fire, and asked who among them would leap into the flames to become the new sun. The proud and wealthy god Tecuciztecatl volunteered but flinched four times at the edge of the blaze. Then the humble, sickly Nanahuatzin, covered in sores, ran forward without hesitation and cast himself into the fire, and it was he who rose transformed as the brilliant sun, while the shamed Tecuciztecatl became only the paler moon.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, was among the most beloved gods of Mesoamerica, a patron of wind, learning, and the priesthood. One myth tells how, after the fourth world ended, Quetzalcoatl descended into the underworld to recover the bones of the dead. The lord of the dead set him cruel obstacles, and the bones broke as he fled with them. Quetzalcoatl ground the fragments into a powder, sprinkled it with his own blood, and from that mixture the people of the present age were born.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: The Aztecs held that the sun did not move of its own strength but had to be fed. Each day the sun god Huitzilopochtli waged war across the sky against the stars and the moon, and only the precious fluid of human blood could give him the power to triumph and rise again. This belief lay behind the practice of human sacrifice, understood not as cruelty but as cosmic obligation, the human share of the work of keeping the sun alight and the world from sliding back into the dark.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: Tezcatlipoca, the smoking mirror, was the dark and powerful god of night, sorcery, and destiny, an unpredictable deity who tempted, tested, and brought low both mortals and gods. He carried an obsidian mirror in place of one foot, said to have been bitten off by the earth monster, and in its black surface he could see all that happened in the world. His ancient rivalry with Quetzalcoatl shaped the myths, as the two gods alternately built up the worlds and tore them down.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: Before the sky and earth were made, there was only the vast monster Cipactli, a creature part crocodile, part fish, and part toad, swimming through the primordial waters with mouths at every joint of her body. Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl seized her and tore her in two, lifting one half to become the heavens and pressing the other down to form the earth. The land itself was her body, and to repay the violence done to her, the gods decreed that the earth must be fed with hearts and watered with blood.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: The Maya Popol Vuh tells how the gods tried more than once to make beings who could speak and worship them. They shaped people first of mud, but the mud figures could not stand or think and dissolved away. Next they carved people of wood, who walked and multiplied but had no hearts or memory and forgot their makers, and so they were destroyed by a flood and by their own animals and tools turning against them. Only when the gods used ground maize did they create true human beings.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: The Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, descended into Xibalba, the Maya underworld, to avenge their father against its sinister lords. The lords of death set them deadly trials in houses of darkness, cold, jaguars, fire, and bats, and the twins survived each by their wit. At last they tricked the lords into ordering their own destruction, and having conquered death, the twins rose into the sky to become the sun and the moon.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: Tlaloc, the Aztec god of rain and lightning, ruled a paradise called Tlalocan, a green realm of eternal spring and abundance. Those who died by drowning, by lightning, or from water-borne diseases were claimed by Tlaloc and went to dwell in this lush afterworld rather than the grim underworld of Mictlan. The god was generous with rain but also fearsome, and the Aztecs offered children to him in the belief that their tears would bring the storms the crops desperately needed.

subtopic: Aztec and Mesoamerican cosmology
sentence: The destination of an Aztec soul depended not on virtue but on the manner of death. Warriors who fell in battle and women who died in childbirth accompanied the sun across the sky. The drowned went to Tlaloc's green paradise. But the vast majority of the dead, those who died ordinary deaths, faced a four-year journey through the nine levels of Mictlan, crossing rivers, mountains that clashed together, and a place of cutting winds, before reaching the silent realm of the death god Mictlantecuhtli.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: In the beginning the cosmos was a featureless egg, and within it slept the giant Pangu for eighteen thousand years. When he woke and stretched, the egg cracked, and the light clear matter floated up to become the sky while the heavy turbid matter sank to form the earth. Pangu stood between them, growing taller each day to hold them apart. When at last he died, his breath became the wind, his eyes the sun and moon, his blood the rivers, and the fleas on his body became the human race.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The goddess Nuwa, with the body of a serpent and the face of a woman, grew lonely in the early world and resolved to make companions. She knelt by a riverbank and shaped little figures from the yellow clay, and each one came to life and danced around her. The work was slow, so she dipped a cord in the mud and flicked it, and the splattered droplets became people too. Thus, the legend says, the nobility were the carefully sculpted ones and the common folk were born from the scattered drops.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: When a war between gods cracked one of the pillars holding up the sky, the heavens tilted and tore, fires raged and floods poured through the gap. The goddess Nuwa took pity on the suffering world. She gathered stones of five colors, melted them in a great fire, and patched the broken sky with the molten paste. To prop up the fallen corner she cut the legs from a giant turtle and set them as new pillars at the four directions, and so she repaired the world a second time after she had made it.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: Long ago ten suns dwelt in a vast mulberry tree at the edge of the eastern sea, and each day one of them crossed the sky in turn. But one morning all ten rose together, and their combined heat scorched the crops, dried the rivers, and threatened to end all life. The mighty archer Houyi was sent to set the world right. He drew his great bow and shot down nine of the suns one after another, leaving a single sun to light the sky, and the parched earth was saved.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: As a reward for shooting down the suns, the archer Houyi was given an elixir of immortality, enough for one person to ascend to heaven. He meant to share a divided dose with his wife Chang'e so they might be together forever as mortals, but Chang'e, alone and tempted, swallowed the whole elixir at once. Made too light for the earth, she drifted up and up until she came to rest upon the cold moon, where she dwells still with only a jade rabbit for company, and where the Chinese still look for her at the Mid-Autumn Festival.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The legendary emperor Yu the Great earned his title by mastering the catastrophic floods that had drowned the early kingdom for generations. His father had tried and failed by building dams to block the waters and was executed for it. Yu chose instead to work with the flood rather than against it, dredging channels and digging canals to guide the water safely to the sea. The labor consumed thirteen years, during which Yu passed the door of his own home three times without once stepping inside to rest.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The Yellow Emperor, Huangdi, was revered as the ancestor of the Chinese people and the founder of civilization itself. The legends credit his reign with the invention of the wheeled cart, the calendar, writing, music, and the healing arts. He was said to have fought a terrible war against the monstrous Chiyou, a rebel with a bronze head and a body of iron, defeating him at last with the help of a goddess and a marvelous chariot that always pointed south, guiding the imperial army through Chiyou's magical fog.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: Chinese folklore holds that an ox-headed god named Shennong, the Divine Farmer, taught humankind agriculture and the use of medicinal plants. To discover which herbs could heal and which could kill, Shennong tasted hundreds of plants himself, and a transparent body or a special insight allowed him to observe their effects within him. The legend says he was finally poisoned by a plant whose toxin he could not counter, dying a martyr to the knowledge he had gathered for the benefit of all who came after.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The tale of the cowherd Niulang and the weaver girl Zhinu is among the most cherished of Chinese legends. Zhinu, a heavenly weaver, descended to earth and married the mortal cowherd, and they lived in happiness with their two children. But the Queen Mother of Heaven, displeased at the union of a goddess and a man, drew a great river of stars across the sky to part them. Once each year, on the seventh night of the seventh month, a bridge of magpies forms across the Milky Way and the lovers may meet for a single day.

subtopic: Chinese myths and legendary emperors
sentence: The dragon of Chinese mythology bears little resemblance to the fire-breathing monster of the West. It is a benevolent, serpentine being associated with water, rain, rivers, and the sea, and with imperial authority itself, so that the emperor sat upon a dragon throne. The Dragon Kings ruled the four seas and the waters of the world, and a community suffering drought would beg the local dragon for rain. To dream of a dragon, or to be born in its year, was considered a sign of great fortune.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: Across medieval Europe, the werewolf was a creature of dread, a person who by curse, witchcraft, or a pact with darkness took the form and hunger of a wolf. Some traditions held that a man became a werewolf by donning a belt of wolf-skin or by sleeping outdoors on a Friday under a full moon. Once transformed, the werewolf was driven to hunt and kill, and the only certain remedy was to wound the beast, for the same injury would appear on the human body and reveal the secret of its dual nature.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: The Greek myth of Lycaon gave the werewolf its very name. Lycaon, king of Arcadia, doubted that Zeus was truly a god, and to test the disguised visitor he served him a dish made from the flesh of a slaughtered human. Enraged by the monstrous crime, Zeus transformed the king on the spot into a wolf, leaving his eyes still burning with their old cruelty and his jaws hungry for blood. From Lycaon's name came the word lycanthropy, the affliction of becoming a wolf.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: In the Norse sagas the warrior could take on the spirit of a beast. The berserkers fought in the frenzy of the bear, and the ulfhednar, the wolf-coats, wore wolf-skins and were said to be possessed by the wolf's ferocity in battle. The saga of the Volsungs tells of Sigmund and his son Sinfjotli, who found enchanted wolf-skins, put them on, and could not remove them for ten days, during which they roamed the forest as savage wolves and killed any who crossed their path.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: The selkie of Scottish and Irish island lore was a seal that could shed its skin and walk ashore as a beautiful human. The classic tale tells of a fisherman who came upon a selkie woman dancing on the rocks, stole and hid her sealskin, and so compelled her to remain with him as his wife. She bore his children and seemed content, but the sea was always in her, and the day a child found the hidden skin, she slipped it on and returned to the waves, never to walk on land again.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: The swan maiden is a shapeshifter found in folktales across northern Europe. She and her sisters fly down to a lake, set aside their swan-feathered cloaks, and bathe as women. A watching man steals one cloak, and the maiden, unable to fly, becomes his wife. The story almost always ends the same way: years later she recovers the hidden feather garment, puts it on, and rises into the sky, sometimes calling her husband to follow on an impossible quest if he would win her back.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: French folklore feared the loup-garou, and the Baltic and Slavic lands told of werewolves with their own variations. In some traditions the werewolf was not always a villain. Tales from the eastern Baltic spoke of werewolves who descended into hell to recover stolen crops and bring fertility back to the fields, fighting the witches who had carried it away. For these communities the man-wolf was a kind of agrarian champion, his nocturnal transformation a service to the harvest rather than a crime.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: The hare was a common shape for the European witch to assume, and country folk held many beliefs about it. A hare seen lingering near a dairy was suspected of being a witch come to steal the milk. The proven cure was a silver bullet or a charge of silver buttons, for ordinary lead could not harm a witch-hare. If a hunted hare escaped into a cottage and a woman within was found gasping or wounded in the same place the shot had struck, the village had its witch.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: The Norse goddess Freyja owned a falcon cloak, a feathered garment that allowed its wearer to take the shape of a bird and fly between the worlds. When the giant Thrym stole Thor's hammer, it was the cloak that the gods borrowed so a messenger could fly to the land of giants and discover where the weapon was hidden.
