Shapeshifting in Norse myth was less a curse than a tool, a power kept in the wardrobes of the gods and lent out when a crisis demanded swift and secret travel.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: Loki, the trickster of the Norse pantheon, was the most fluid shapeshifter of all. He became a mare to lure away a giant's stallion, and in that form gave birth to Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse of Odin. He became a salmon to escape the gods' vengeance, a fly to torment a sleeping craftsman, and a falcon to undertake his schemes. For Loki, no single shape was ever true, and his endless transformations mirrored a nature that no oath or loyalty could ever pin down.

subtopic: European werewolf and shapeshifter lore
sentence: In the Welsh Mabinogi, the magicians Math and Gwydion punished the brothers Gilfaethwy and Gwydion for a grievous crime by transforming them into pairs of animals. For one year they lived as a stag and a hind, for the next as a boar and a sow, and for the third as a pair of wolves, and in each form they bred and brought forth offspring. Only after three years of bestial shape and shame were they restored to human form, having learned through the body what their human minds had refused.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: When a Greek died, the soul travelled to the realm of Hades, and to enter it the shade had to cross the river Styx. The ferryman Charon waited on the bank, and he would carry only those who could pay his fee, a coin placed upon or beneath the tongue of the corpse before burial. The unburied and the penniless were turned away to wander the gloomy shore for a hundred years, which is why the Greeks regarded a proper burial as a sacred and absolute duty owed to the dead.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: Orpheus, the greatest of all musicians, descended into the underworld to reclaim his wife Eurydice, who had died of a serpent's bite. His music was so heartbreakingly beautiful that the wheel of Ixion stood still, the tormented dead forgot their pain, and even the iron heart of Hades was moved. The god granted Orpheus his wish, but on one condition: that he walk ahead of Eurydice toward the light and not look back at her until both had reached the world above.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: Orpheus climbed the long dark path toward the daylight, listening for the footsteps of Eurydice behind him, but the underworld was silent and he heard nothing. As he stepped at last into the light, doubt overcame him, and he turned to see if she truly followed. She did, but she had not yet crossed the threshold, and at his glance she slipped backward into the dark with a final faint farewell. Orpheus had lost her a second time, and this time forever.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: The underworld held a place of punishment called Tartarus, where the greatest sinners suffered torments shaped to fit their crimes. Tantalus, who had served the gods his own son, stood forever in a pool that receded when he stooped to drink, beneath fruit that the wind swept beyond his grasp. Sisyphus, who had cheated death itself, was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill, only to watch it tumble down each time he neared the summit, an endless and meaningless labor.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: Persephone, daughter of the harvest goddess Demeter, was gathering flowers in a meadow when the earth split open and Hades carried her down to be his queen. Demeter's grief was so terrible that the crops withered and famine threatened the world. Zeus commanded Persephone's return, but because she had eaten a few pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she was bound to it. The compromise gave her to her mother for part of the year and to Hades for the rest, and her annual descent became the coming of winter.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: The hero Theseus and his friend Pirithous made the most reckless of all journeys to the underworld. Pirithous, in his arrogance, wished to take Persephone herself as a bride, and the two descended to Hades to seize the queen of the dead. Hades received them with deceptive courtesy and invited them to sit, and the moment they did, the Chair of Forgetfulness bound them fast. Pirithous remained trapped forever, and Theseus was freed only when Heracles, passing through on his own labor, tore him from the stone.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: The souls of the dead in Hades were not punished by default; most simply existed as pale, witless shades, drifting and twittering like bats in the gloom. When Odysseus sailed to the edge of the world and dug a trench of sacrificial blood to summon the dead, the shades that gathered could not speak or recognize him until they had drunk of the blood. Only then did memory and voice return to them briefly, and even the spirit of the great Achilles confessed he would rather be a poor man's servant alive than a king among the dead.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: After crossing the Styx, the souls of the dead came before three judges, Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus, kings in life who had been chosen for their justice. They sorted the dead by the lives they had led. The wicked were sent down to Tartarus to suffer, the ordinary went to the Asphodel Meadows to drift in gray monotony, and the heroes and the virtuous were granted entry to the Elysian Fields, a land of soft light and gentle breezes where the blessed dead knew peace.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: The river Lethe wound through the underworld, and its name meant forgetfulness. The dead who drank from it lost all memory of their former lives. In the traditions that taught reincarnation, this was a necessary step: a soul destined to be born again first had to drink the waters of Lethe so that it would enter its new life unburdened by the recollection of the old. To remember a past life was the rare and uncanny exception, the sign of a soul that had somehow slipped past the river.

subtopic: Greek underworld and journeys of the dead
sentence: When Heracles undertook his final labor, the capture of Cerberus, he first had to be initiated into the sacred mysteries so that he might enter the land of the dead and return alive. Guided by Hermes and Athena, he descended through the cave at Taenarum. In the underworld he met the shade of Meleager and promised to marry his sister, freed Theseus from the Chair of Forgetfulness, and even wounded Hades himself in the shoulder before wrestling the great hound into submission and dragging it up to the light.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: The Dreaming, or Dreamtime, is the foundational concept of Aboriginal Australian belief, describing the era when ancestral beings emerged from the formless earth and shaped the world. As these great beings travelled across the land, they created the mountains, rivers, waterholes, and living things, and they laid down the law and the customs that people were to follow. The Dreaming is not a past that ended; it is understood as an eternal present, woven into the land itself and renewed through story, song, and ceremony.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: The Rainbow Serpent is among the most widespread ancestral beings of Aboriginal Australia, a vast snake associated with water, rain, and the deep waterholes that never run dry. As it moved through the soft early earth, its winding body gouged out the courses of the rivers and the great gorges. The Rainbow Serpent is both creator and guardian, generous with water and life but dangerous when angered, and its arc still appears in the sky after rain as a sign of its enduring presence.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: A widely told Dreaming story explains how the birds first received their colors, when all birds were once a dull and uniform black. A small bird hurt its foot, and the wound festered until it swelled and finally burst. From it spilled a brilliant spray of color, and the other birds rushed to bathe themselves in the bright fluid, each taking a different hue. Only the crow held back, and so the crow alone remained black, while the parrots, finches, and lorikeets carried their dazzling colors away.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: Many Dreaming stories of central Australia tell of the Seven Sisters, a group of ancestral women pursued endlessly across the land and sky by a man who desired them. The sisters fled from waterhole to waterhole, and the man followed, and their long chase carved sacred sites into the country wherever they paused. At last the sisters rose into the heavens to escape him, becoming the cluster of stars known elsewhere as the Pleiades, while their pursuer became a nearby star, still following them across the night.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: A Dreaming story of southeastern Australia tells how fire was once hoarded by the water-rat, or by a band of women, who kept it hidden and refused to share. Various tellings name a different hero, but the pattern holds: a clever ancestral being, often a bird, steals or tricks the fire away from those who selfishly kept it. The fire is then placed within the heart of certain trees, so that ever after people can draw it out by rubbing wood together, and warmth and cooking belong to everyone.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: Tiddalik the frog grew so thirsty one morning that he drank up all the fresh water in the world, swelling to an enormous size, and the land began to wither and die without it. The other animals, parched and desperate, knew that the only way to recover the water was to make Tiddalik laugh. They gathered before him and tried every trick they knew, until at last the eel twisted itself into such ridiculous knots and shapes that the great frog burst out laughing, and the water gushed forth to fill the rivers and lakes once more.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: Songlines, sometimes called dreaming tracks, are the routes across the Australian land travelled by the ancestral beings during the Dreaming. Each songline is recorded in a sequence of songs that describe the landmarks along the way, the waterholes, the ridges, the resting places. To sing the song in order is to know the path, and so the songlines served as both sacred narrative and a precise map, allowing knowledgeable travelers to cross vast and seemingly featureless country by following the words of the ancestors.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: A Dreaming story tells how the kangaroo got its pouch. A mother kangaroo, in a time of great drought, showed kindness to an old and weak wombat, leading the lost creature to water and food without knowing it was an ancestral being in disguise. As a reward for her selflessness, the spirit gave her a soft pouch in which she could carry and protect her young. The grateful kangaroo became the first of her kind to bear a pouch, and all her descendants carry it still.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: Among the Yolngu people of Arnhem Land, the two Wagilag Sisters are central ancestral figures whose journey shaped the land and established sacred law and ceremony. As the sisters travelled, naming the plants and animals they encountered, they came upon the waterhole of the great Rainbow Serpent. The serpent rose, swallowed the sisters and their child, and later disgorged them, and from this powerful and dangerous encounter came the patterns of ritual that the Yolngu maintain to this day.

subtopic: Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime stories
sentence: A Dreaming story explains why the emu cannot fly. In the early time the emu and the brolga were rivals, and the brolga, jealous of the emu's beautiful wings, tricked her. The brolga concealed her own chicks but pretended she had eaten all but two, claiming she flew better and faster without the burden of so many. The proud emu, not to be outdone, cut off her own great wings. The brolga then revealed her hidden brood, and the wingless emu, deceived and grounded forever, was left to run upon the earth.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: The Kalevala opens with the creation of the world from the fragments of a great egg. The maiden of the air, Ilmatar, drifted upon the primordial sea, and a teal laid its eggs upon her knee. When the eggs rolled into the water and broke, the lower shell became the earth and the upper shell the dome of the sky, the yolk became the sun and the white the moon, and the speckled fragments became the stars scattered across the heavens.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: Vainamoinen, the central hero of the Kalevala, was no warrior but a sage and a singer, born already old and wise from the womb of Ilmatar after centuries within her. His power lay in song and the knowledge of origins, for in Finnish belief, to know the true beginning of any thing was to command it. With his songs he could raise storms, calm seas, and sink a rival into a bog up to his very chin, and his voice was the deepest magic in the world.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: The Sampo was a mysterious and miraculous object forged by the smith Ilmarinen, a magical mill that ground out grain, salt, and gold without ceasing, an inexhaustible source of prosperity. Ilmarinen made it as a bride-price for the daughter of Louhi, the fearsome mistress of the cold northern land of Pohjola. The Sampo brought such abundance to Pohjola that the heroes of Kalevala resolved to steal it back, and the struggle over the wondrous mill drove the great conflict of the epic.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: Ilmarinen, the eternal smith of the Kalevala, was the craftsman who had forged the very dome of the sky, hammering it so finely that no trace of the tongs or the blows could be seen. He was the maker of the Sampo and of countless wonders, yet his greatest sorrow was love. When his wife was killed, the grieving smith forged himself a bride of gold and silver, but the metal woman lay cold beside him in the night, and he learned that no craft, however perfect, could forge a living heart.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: To complete a magic spell, Vainamoinen needed three lost words of power, and he was told they could be found only in the belly of the dead giant Antero Vipunen. The hero journeyed to where the giant lay buried under the earth, trees growing from his shoulders, and forced his way into the giant's mouth. From within Vipunen's body Vainamoinen tormented him, forging iron in his stomach, until the giant, to be rid of his tormentor, sang out all the ancient words and origin-spells he had ever known.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: The tragic figure of the Kalevala is Kullervo, a youth cursed from birth, the sole survivor of a slaughtered family, sold into slavery and abused at every turn. Possessed of vast and uncontrollable strength, everything he touched turned to ruin. When he unknowingly seduced his own lost sister, who threw herself into a river upon learning the truth, Kullervo's despair became total. After avenging himself on those who had wronged him, he asked his own sword whether it would slay him, and the blade consented.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: Lemminkainen was the reckless, charming, and womanizing hero of the Kalevala, forever rushing into danger his elders warned him against. Seeking the hand of a maiden of Pohjola, he was set deadly tasks, and in attempting to shoot the swan of the river of the dead, he was himself killed and his body cut to pieces and thrown into the dark waters. His mother, refusing to accept his death, raked the river until she had recovered every fragment, then sewed him back together and sang the life back into him.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: Louhi, the mistress of Pohjola, was the great adversary of the Kalevala, a powerful sorceress who ruled the cold and misty land of the north. When the heroes stole the Sampo, Louhi pursued them across the sea, transforming herself into a monstrous eagle with warriors gripped in her talons. In the battle that followed the Sampo was shattered and lost beneath the waves, but its broken fragments washed ashore, and from them, the epic says, came the lasting fertility and fortune of the land of Kalevala.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: The Kalevala was not an ancient text passed down whole, but a great epic assembled in the nineteenth century by the physician Elias Lonnrot. He travelled through the rural districts of Finland and Karelia, listening to elderly singers who still performed the old runic songs, the oral poetry of charms, origins, and heroes. Lonnrot collected, selected, and stitched these scattered songs into a continuous narrative, giving Finland a national epic drawn from a folk tradition that had survived only in living memory.

subtopic: Finnish Kalevala and shamanic heroes
sentence: At the close of the Kalevala, the old age of magic and song begins to give way. A virgin named Marjatta bears a child after eating a lingonberry, and when the boy is two weeks old, Vainamoinen judges that an illegitimate child should be put to death. But the infant rebukes the old hero for his harsh and unjust verdict, and the child is baptized king of Karelia. Vainamoinen, recognizing that his time has passed, sails away in a copper boat, leaving behind only his songs and his kantele for the people.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The siren of Greek myth was not the gentle mermaid of later imagination but a deadly creature, part woman and part bird, who perched on rocky islands and sang with irresistible sweetness. Their song lured sailors to steer toward the voice, and ship after ship was wrecked upon the reefs, the shore white with the bones of the dead. Odysseus, warned by the witch Circe, had his crew stop their ears with wax and bind him to the mast, so that he alone heard the song and survived to tell of it.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: Mami Wata is a water spirit venerated across West and Central Africa and carried into the Caribbean and the Americas by the African diaspora. She is most often pictured as a beautiful woman with the lower body of a fish or with a great serpent draped around her, holding a mirror and a comb. Mami Wata is associated with wealth, beauty, healing, and danger, a bringer of good fortune to her devotees and a perilous seductress to those who break faith with her.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: Scottish folklore feared the kelpie, a shapeshifting water horse that haunted the rivers and lochs. The kelpie often appeared on the bank as a fine, gentle horse, tempting weary travelers to climb upon its back. The moment a rider was seated, the creature's hide turned adhesive, the rider could not dismount, and the kelpie plunged into the deep water to drown and devour its prey. Some tales said only the liver was left to float ashore, a grim warning to others.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The merrow was the mermaid of Irish folklore, and unlike many water spirits she was often gentle toward humankind. The merrow wore a magic cap, the cohuleen druith, which allowed her to travel through the water, and a man who found and hid the cap could keep a merrow ashore as his bride. Yet the sea always called to her, and like the selkie wife of Scotland, the merrow who recovered her cap would slip back beneath the waves, leaving her human family behind.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: In Slavic folklore the vodyanitsa or vodyanoy's female counterpart, and in some regions a kind of rusalka, were the water maidens of rivers and lakes. The Germanic peoples told of the nixie, a water sprite who might appear as a beautiful woman combing her long hair by the water's edge or as a handsome man playing a fiddle. The nixie's music could draw the unwary into the deep, and parents warned their children that a friendly stranger met beside the river might not be human at all.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The legend of Melusine spread through medieval France and beyond, telling of a beautiful woman who agreed to marry a nobleman on one condition: that he never look upon her on a Saturday. For years they prospered and she bore him many children, until at last his curiosity or jealousy overcame him. Spying on her in her bath, he saw that from the waist down she had the tail of a serpent. The secret broken, Melusine cried out, transformed fully into a dragon, and flew from the castle forever.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: Japanese tradition tells of the ningyo, a fish-like creature with a human face, whose flesh was said to grant extraordinarily long life to anyone who ate it. The legend of Yao Bikuni tells of a girl who unknowingly ate the flesh of a ningyo and ceased to age, watching her husbands and friends grow old and die for eight hundred years. To weep was the ningyo's other power, and to catch one or hear it cry was held to be an omen of storm and misfortune.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: The rusalki of Slavic lands sat in the branches of willows overhanging the water, combing their long green or pale hair. In the older belief they were the spirits of the drowned, restless and dangerous, capable of luring and tickling a victim to death. During Rusalka Week the village kept careful customs, leaving offerings and avoiding swimming, for the water maidens were abroad. The folklore wove together a fear of drowning, the dangers of the river, and the grief for young women who had died too soon.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: Sailors of the European age of exploration carried mermaid lore across every ocean, and ships' logs recorded sightings that were almost certainly manatees and dugongs glimpsed at a distance. The mermaid in maritime belief was an ambiguous omen. To see one might foretell a coming storm or a shipwreck, yet a mermaid could also be persuaded to grant calm seas or a wish in exchange for a kindness. Like the sea itself, she was beautiful and treacherous, generous and merciless by turns.

subtopic: Mermaids and water spirits worldwide
sentence: In the folklore of the Philippines, the sirena dwells in the sea and the rivers, a half-fish enchantress whose song lures fishermen and swimmers to a watery death. Her freshwater kin, the siyokoy, was imagined as a scaly, gilled merman, more monstrous than beautiful. Coastal communities told these stories partly as warnings about the genuine perils of deep and fast water, dressing the dangers of drowning in the shape of a singing creature who would not let her victims go.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: The gods of Asgard knew their own ending was foretold. Ragnarok would begin with Fimbulwinter, three years of unbroken winter with no summer between them, when the snow drove from every direction and the world grew cold and dark. Brother would betray brother, kinship would count for nothing, and an age of axes and swords would come before the final battle. The Norse did not imagine their gods as deathless; they imagined them as doomed and fighting bravely anyway.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: At Ragnarok the great wolf Fenrir, bound long ago by the gods with a magic fetter, would finally break free. His lower jaw would scrape the earth and his upper jaw the sky, and fire would burn from his eyes and nostrils. Odin, the All-Father, would ride out to meet him, and despite all his wisdom and his deathless spear, the wolf would swallow the chief of the gods whole. Then Odin's son Vidar would step forward to avenge his father, tearing the wolf's jaws apart with his great boot.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Thor and the Midgard Serpent, ancient enemies, would meet for the last time at Ragnarok. The serpent Jormungandr, whose coiled body encircled the whole world, would rise from the sea spewing venom across the sky and water. Thor would battle the great snake and at last strike it dead with his hammer. But the thunder god would manage only nine steps from the serpent's corpse before the poison flooding his veins brought him down, and so the mightiest of the gods would die in his moment of victory.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: The fire giant Surtr would come from the burning south at Ragnarok, his flaming sword brighter than the sun. He would advance across the shattered rainbow bridge and onto the field of Vigrid, where the last battle was fought. After the gods had fallen, Surtr would fling fire across all the nine worlds, and the flames would consume Yggdrasil, the homes of gods and men alike, until the scorched earth sank at last beneath the boiling sea.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Loki, long bound in punishment for engineering the death of Baldr, would slip free of his chains at Ragnarok and take his place against the gods. He would steer the ship Naglfar, built from the untrimmed nails of the dead, carrying an army of giants to the final battle. On the field of Vigrid, Loki and the watchman Heimdall, ancient adversaries, would meet and slay one another, each falling to the other's blade as the world burned around them.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: The death of Baldr was the first sign that Ragnarok was near. Baldr the beautiful, the gentlest of the gods, dreamed of his own death, and his mother Frigg made every thing in the world swear never to harm him, overlooking only the humble mistletoe. Loki discovered the omission, fashioned a dart of mistletoe, and guided the hand of the blind god Hodr to throw it. Baldr fell dead, and the gods' grief was the grief of those who knew their bright age had begun to end.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Ragnarok was not the end of all things but the end of one age. After the fire and the flood, a new and green earth would rise fresh from the sea, watered and fertile, where fields would bear grain unsown. A few of the gods would survive: Vidar and Vali, and Thor's sons Modi and Magni, who would inherit their father's hammer. Baldr himself would return from the dead. The story of the doom of the gods was, in the end, also a story of renewal.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Heimdall's horn would sound the alarm of Ragnarok. The watchman of the gods, who needed no more sleep than a bird and could see for a hundred leagues by day or night, kept the Gjallarhorn ready at the foot of the rainbow bridge. When he saw the forces of chaos massing for the assault on Asgard, he would lift the horn to his lips and blow a blast so loud it would ring through all the nine worlds, and every god and every fallen warrior in Valhalla would know the final hour had come.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Odin gathered the bravest of slain warriors into Valhalla precisely so that they would fight beside the gods at Ragnarok. The Valkyries chose the worthy dead from every battlefield and carried them to the great hall, where they feasted and fought each day in preparation. Yet the gods knew the outcome was already fixed; the einherjar would march out to die alongside their patrons. The Norse vision of the afterlife was not a reward but a recruitment for a battle that could not be won.

subtopic: Norse Ragnarok and the doom of the gods
sentence: Before Ragnarok the sky itself would be devoured. The wolves Skoll and Hati, who had chased the sun and the moon across the heavens since the world began, would at last overtake their prey. Skoll would swallow the sun and Hati the moon, and the stars would vanish from the sky, plunging the earth into total darkness. The cosmos that the gods had so carefully built from the body of Ymir would come apart piece by piece, the lights extinguished, the bonds broken, the long order ending.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: The Trojan War sprang from a single act of vanity at a wedding feast. The goddess of discord, Eris, uninvited and resentful, threw among the guests a golden apple inscribed for the fairest. Three goddesses, Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, each claimed it, and Zeus wisely refused to judge between them. The choice fell instead to the Trojan prince Paris, and each goddess offered him a bribe. Paris chose Aphrodite's gift, the love of the most beautiful woman in the world, and so doomed his city.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: The most beautiful woman in the world was Helen, and she was already the wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. When Paris carried her away to Troy, Menelaus called upon the oath sworn by all of Helen's former suitors to defend the marriage of whoever won her. A vast Greek fleet gathered, a thousand ships under the command of Menelaus's brother Agamemnon, and sailed for Troy to take Helen back by force, beginning a siege that would last ten long years.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: Achilles was the greatest of the Greek warriors, the son of a sea goddess who had dipped him as a baby in the river Styx to make him invulnerable. But she had held him by the heel, and that one spot the water never touched. It was foretold that Achilles could live a long and unremembered life, or a short and glorious one at Troy. He chose glory, and his name has never been forgotten, though he fell at last to an arrow guided into his vulnerable heel.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: The wrath of Achilles is the theme that opens the Iliad. When Agamemnon seized a captive woman that Achilles considered his rightful prize, the proud warrior withdrew from the fighting and sulked in his tent, and the Greeks suffered terribly without him. Only the death of his beloved companion Patroclus, killed by the Trojan prince Hector while wearing Achilles's own armor, drew the hero back to war, blazing with a grief-stricken fury that nothing could now restrain.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: Hector was the noblest defender of Troy, the city's greatest warrior and the eldest son of King Priam. Unlike Paris, whose folly had brought the war, Hector fought for duty and for the protection of his family and his people. In one of the most moving scenes of the Iliad, he bids farewell to his wife Andromache and his infant son on the city walls, knowing he may not return, before going down to meet Achilles in the duel that he knows will end his life.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: After slaying Hector, Achilles dishonored the body, dragging it behind his chariot around the walls of Troy day after day. Then old King Priam, alone and unarmed, came by night through the Greek camp to the tent of the man who had killed his son. He knelt and kissed the hands of Achilles and begged for the body's return. The two enemies wept together, one for a slain son and one for his own father far away, and Achilles, his rage finally spent, gave Hector back for burial.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: Troy did not fall to force but to a trick devised by the cunning Odysseus. The Greeks built an enormous hollow horse of wood, hid their finest warriors inside it, and sailed away as if abandoning the siege, leaving the horse before the gates as an offering. Despite warnings, the Trojans dragged the great horse into their city and celebrated their apparent victory. In the dark of night the warriors crept out, opened the gates to the returned army, and Troy was put to the sword and the torch.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: The priest Laocoon warned the Trojans against the wooden horse, crying that he feared the Greeks even when they brought gifts, and he hurled his spear against its hollow flank. But the gods had decreed Troy's fall, and as Laocoon stood at the altar, two monstrous serpents rose from the sea, coiled around the priest and his two young sons, and crushed them all to death. The Trojans, taking the omen as punishment for the spear-throw, hauled the horse inside, sealing their doom.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: Cassandra, daughter of King Priam, was cursed with a terrible gift. The god Apollo, in love with her, granted her the power of true prophecy, but when she refused his advances, he could not take the gift back and instead twisted it: she would always foresee the truth, and no one would ever believe her. Cassandra foretold the fall of Troy, warned against the wooden horse, and saw her own death coming, yet her warnings were dismissed as the ravings of a madwoman.

subtopic: Trojan War legends and heroes
sentence: Not all the heroes of Troy were Greek. The Trojan prince Aeneas, a son of the goddess Aphrodite, survived the fall of the city. The legend, given its grandest form in Virgil's Aeneid, tells how Aeneas carried his aged father on his back and led a band of survivors out of the burning ruins. After long wanderings across the Mediterranean, he came at last to Italy, where his descendants would found the city of Rome, so that from the ashes of Troy a greater empire was said to rise.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The foundation myth of Korea tells of Hwanung, the son of the heavenly god, who descended to a mountaintop with three thousand followers to govern the human world. A bear and a tiger came to him, longing to become human. Hwanung gave them sacred mugwort and twenty cloves of garlic and told them to eat only this and avoid the sunlight for one hundred days. The tiger lacked the patience and gave up, but the bear endured, and after twenty-one days was transformed into a woman.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The bear-woman of the founding legend, called Ungnyeo, longed for a child, and Hwanung, moved by her devotion, took human form and married her. Their son was Dangun, who is said to have founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon, in ancient times and to have ruled it for many centuries before withdrawing to become a mountain god. Koreans long honored Dangun as the legendary ancestor of their nation, the human child of a heavenly god and a bear who had willed herself into a woman.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The kingdom of Silla had its own birth legend. The elders of the six villages, seeking a king, saw a strange light by a well and found there a great red egg, and beside it a horse that knelt and then flew up into the sky. From the egg came a radiant boy, and they named him Bak Hyeokgeose and raised him to be their first sovereign. His queen was said to have been born from the rib of a dragon, and together they ruled the young kingdom in peace.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The gumiho is the nine-tailed fox of Korean folklore, a fox that has lived a thousand years and gained the power to take the shape of a beautiful woman. Unlike the kitsune of Japan, the gumiho of older Korean tales was almost always dangerous, a creature said to need human livers or hearts to survive. Some legends offered her a path to becoming fully human, often requiring her to abstain from killing for a thousand days, a test of restraint that the stories rarely allowed her to complete.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: A beloved Korean folktale tells of two brothers, the greedy elder Nolbu and the kind younger Heungbu. Heungbu mended the broken leg of a swallow, and the grateful bird returned with a magic gourd seed that grew to yield treasure and rescued the poor man from want. The envious Nolbu deliberately broke a swallow's leg to win the same reward, but the gourd he grew burst open to release goblins, filth, and ruin. The tale rewards compassion and punishes the greed that would manufacture a kindness for profit.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The dokkaebi are the goblins of Korean folklore, mischievous and sometimes frightening spirits often said to arise from old discarded objects stained with human blood. A dokkaebi carries a magic club that can summon anything its owner wishes, and the creatures love games, riddles, and wrestling matches. They are not purely evil; a dokkaebi might reward a virtuous person with wealth or punish a wicked one, and they can be outwitted, for they are easily distracted and oddly fond of fairness in a contest.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The tale of Shim Cheong is one of the great stories of Korean filial devotion. Shim Cheong was the daughter of a blind man, and she learned that his sight could be restored if three hundred sacks of rice were offered to a temple. Having no money, she sold herself to sailors who needed a maiden to sacrifice to the sea dragon. She threw herself into the waves, but the Dragon King, moved by her devotion, sent her back to the world inside a lotus flower, and she rose to become a queen and find her father again.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The founder of the Goguryeo kingdom was Jumong, a legendary archer whose name meant skilled bowman. His mother was a daughter of a river god, impregnated by sunlight, and Jumong was born from an egg. Persecuted by jealous princes, he fled south on horseback, and when a river blocked his escape, he called out his divine ancestry, and fish and turtles rose to the surface and formed a living bridge so that he could cross. On the far side he founded the kingdom that would become one of the great powers of the peninsula.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: Korean folklore tells of the woodcutter and the fairy, a heavenly maiden who came down with her sisters to bathe in a mountain pool. A woodcutter, advised by a deer he had saved from a hunter, hid her feathered robe so she could not return to heaven, and she became his wife. The deer had warned him not to give back the robe until she had borne three children, but he relented after two, and the fairy, slipping on her recovered robe, gathered her children and floated up to the sky.

subtopic: Korean foundation myths and folk legends
sentence: The Korean creation myth, preserved in shamanic songs, tells how the sky and earth were once joined and were parted by a giant or by the will of a creator god. In one telling there were two suns and two moons, scorching and freezing the early world by turns, until a heroic deity shot down one of each, leaving a single sun and a single moon to balance the seasons. The shaman who sang these origin songs did not merely recite a story but renewed the order of the cosmos through the telling.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: Long before the vampire of gothic novels, the villages of the Balkans feared a coarser, earthier creature. The folk vampire was a recently buried corpse believed to rise and trouble the living, often a person who had died badly, violently, or in sin. A bloated body, a ruddy face, blood at the lips, or hair and nails that seemed to have grown after death were taken as signs that the dead one had become a vampire and was feeding upon the village.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: Serbian folklore gave Europe the word vampire, and one of its most famous cases was the peasant Arnold Paole, who in the early eighteenth century was said to have returned from the grave to torment his neighbors. When the villagers exhumed his body and found it uncorrupted, they drove a stake through the heart, at which the corpse was said to groan and bleed, and then they burned it. Such accounts, recorded by Austrian officials, carried the vampire panic into the wider European imagination.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: Many remedies were used to keep the dead from rising in Balkan villages. A suspected corpse might be buried face down, so that if it tried to claw its way out it would dig itself deeper into the earth. Sharp objects, thorns, or sickles were placed in or around the grave. Some communities scattered seeds or grains of millet in the coffin, in the belief that the vampire would be compelled to count them one by one, an endless task that would keep it occupied until the safety of dawn.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: The Greek vrykolakas was a Balkan undead with traits all its own. It was not always a blood-drinker; instead it was said to wander, knock on doors, and call out the names of the living, and anyone who answered would soon die. For this reason villagers learned never to respond to a knock until it came a second time. The vrykolakas grew stronger the longer it remained, and the surest cure, as in much of the region, was to disinter the corpse and destroy it utterly with fire.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: In Romanian folklore the strigoi was a troubled spirit or revenant, sometimes the soul of a witch, sometimes a corpse that had failed to find rest. A living strigoi was a person born with a caul or with extra features who might leave their body at night to drain the vitality of others. The dead strigoi rose from the grave to plague its own family first. Garlic, holy water, and the careful watching of the dead in the days before burial were the village defenses against it.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: Folk belief held that a person could be marked for vampirism from the very beginning of life. A child born with a caul, born with teeth, born on an unlucky day, or conceived during a forbidden time of the church calendar was thought to be at risk of rising after death. So too were those who had been excommunicated, who had practiced sorcery, or over whose corpse an animal had been allowed to leap. The vampire of folklore was, in part, a way of explaining the unquiet dead and the misfortunes of the living.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: The destruction of a vampire was a grim communal ritual. The grave would be opened, often at the urging of a frightened village, and the corpse examined for the telltale signs of unrest. A stake of hawthorn, ash, or aspen would be driven through the heart, the head sometimes severed and placed between the legs, and the mouth stuffed with garlic or a coin. When even these measures failed to bring peace, the body was hacked apart and burned, and the ashes scattered or thrown into running water.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: The vampire bore a complicated relationship with running water, sunlight, and thresholds in Balkan belief. It was widely held that a vampire could not cross running water, and that it had to return to its grave or its home soil before the cock's crow. The creature could not enter a dwelling unless it was invited, a detail of folklore that placed a measure of safety in the hands of the living, who needed only the wit and the will to refuse the dead a welcome.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: South Slavic tradition told that a vampire might be hunted by a special person born to the task. The dhampir, said to be the child of a vampire and a living woman, was believed to possess the rare ability to see and destroy the undead. Villages plagued by a vampire might summon such a hunter, who would perform a dramatic ritual, often miming a struggle with an invisible enemy, and declare the threat ended. The dhampir's craft was passed down in certain families as a kind of inherited profession.

subtopic: Vampire and undead folklore of the Balkans
sentence: The vampire panics that swept the Balkans were often responses to inexplicable death. When a wave of illness took several members of one family in quick succession, the survivors might conclude that the first to die had risen and was drawing the others into the grave. The exhumation that followed sometimes revealed a corpse that natural decomposition had bloated and discolored, and to people who did not understand the processes of decay, the swollen, blood-flecked body looked exactly like a thing that had fed.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The founding of Rome began with a crime and a betrayal. The twin brothers Romulus and Remus were sons of the war god Mars and a Vestal Virgin, and a fearful king ordered them drowned in the Tiber. The basket carrying them washed ashore, and a she-wolf found the infants and suckled them at her den until a shepherd took them in. Raised to manhood unaware of their royal blood, the twins would grow up to overthrow the usurper and resolve to build a city of their own.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: Romulus and Remus quarreled over where to found their city and which of them should rule it. They agreed to settle the matter by augury, watching the sky for birds, but the omens were disputed. Romulus began to build a wall on the Palatine Hill, and Remus, mocking his brother's effort, leaped contemptuously over the low rampart. In a fury Romulus struck his brother dead, declaring that so would perish anyone who dared to cross his walls, and the city took the name of its surviving, fratricidal founder.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The new city of Rome had warriors but no women, and the neighboring tribes refused to allow their daughters to marry such a band of outlaws. Romulus devised a stratagem. He invited the Sabines to a great festival, and at a signal the Roman men seized the unmarried Sabine women and carried them off. The Sabines returned in war, but when the two armies met, the abducted women, now wives and mothers, threw themselves between the lines, begging their fathers and husbands to make peace.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The god Janus held a unique place in Roman myth, a deity with two faces looking in opposite directions, toward the past and the future, the inside and the outside. He was the god of doorways, gates, beginnings, and transitions, invoked first in any prayer before all other gods. The gates of his temple in the Roman Forum were kept open in time of war and closed only in time of peace, and in the long, warlike history of Rome those gates were closed remarkably few times.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The legend of Romulus did not end with his death but with his disappearance. As the first king reviewed his troops on the Field of Mars, a sudden and violent storm swept over the assembly, hiding him from view in cloud and darkness. When the sky cleared, Romulus was gone, never to be seen again as a mortal. The Romans came to believe he had been carried up to the heavens to become the god Quirinus, and so the founder of the city joined the divine guardians who watched over it.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The Romans honored a goddess Vesta, the keeper of the hearth, and her sacred flame burned perpetually in her round temple in the Forum. Six priestesses, the Vestal Virgins, tended the fire and were bound to chastity for thirty years of service. If the flame went out, it was taken as a dreadful omen of danger to the state, and the negligent priestess was scourged. A Vestal who broke her vow of chastity faced a far worse fate, being entombed alive in a small underground chamber.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: Roman legend told of Numa Pompilius, the second king, a wise and peaceful ruler said to have been instructed in law and religion by the nymph Egeria, whom he met in a sacred grove. Where Romulus had given Rome its walls and its warlike spirit, Numa gave it its calendar, its priesthoods, and its rites. The Romans cherished the contrast, the founder of arms and the founder of religion, as the twin pillars on which their city had been built.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The Lares and Penates were the household gods of every Roman home, the spirits who guarded the family and its store of food. A small shrine, the lararium, stood in the house, and the family made daily offerings to keep the protective spirits content. The Penates watched over the pantry and the inner household, while the Lares guarded the dwelling and its land. A Roman moving to a new home carried these gods with him, for to abandon them was to leave the household defenseless.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: When the Gauls besieged Rome and crept up the steep Capitoline Hill by night, the exhausted defenders slept and even the watchdogs failed to bark. But the sacred geese kept in the temple of Juno heard the intruders and set up a tremendous cackling that woke the garrison in time to hurl the attackers back down the cliff. Ever after the Romans honored the geese of the Capitol, the legend told, and held the watchdogs in disgrace for their silence on that crucial night.

subtopic: Roman myths and the founding of Rome
sentence: The Romans told how the hero Horatius Cocles held the wooden bridge across the Tiber alone against an entire invading army. While his comrades hacked the bridge down behind him, Horatius stood his ground in the narrow gap, holding off the enemy with his sword and shield. When the timbers finally crashed into the river, Horatius, fully armored, plunged into the current and swam to safety, and the city was saved by the courage of a single man who would not yield his ground.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Jewish folklore tells of Lilith, a figure who grew over the centuries from a class of night-demons into a single named being. In one tradition she was Adam's first wife, created from the earth as he was, who refused to be considered his inferior and fled the garden. She became a creature of the night, blamed for the deaths of infants and for troubling sleeping men, and amulets bearing the names of three protective angels were hung above cradles to keep her away.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The golem of Jewish legend was an artificial being formed from clay or earth and animated by sacred words. The most famous tale attaches to Rabbi Loew of sixteenth-century Prague, who was said to have made a golem to protect the Jewish community from persecution. The creature was brought to life by inscribing a holy name, or the Hebrew word for truth, and it could be stilled again by erasing a single letter, turning the word truth into the word death.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The dybbuk of Eastern European Jewish folklore was the restless soul of a dead person, unable to find peace, that entered and possessed the body of a living one. The dybbuk might be a sinner fleeing judgment or a soul with unfinished business in the world. The possessed person would speak with the voice of the dead and act against their own nature, and only a learned rabbi, performing an exorcism with sacred names and the blowing of the ram's horn, could compel the trapped soul to depart.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Folk belief in the Near East held that the very air was thick with unseen spirits, and the shedim were the demons of Jewish lore. They were said to dwell in ruined places, in deserts, and near water, and to be most active at night and at noon. The shedim could cause illness and madness, and a host of practices grew up to ward them off, from amulets and incantations to the custom of not greeting a stranger by a well or of pouring out the first water drawn in the morning.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Asmodeus appears in Jewish folklore as a king of demons, a figure both dangerous and strangely useful. In the tale of Tobit he tormented a young woman, slaying her bridegrooms on their wedding nights, until he was driven off by the smoke of a burned fish heart. In later legends Asmodeus was captured by King Solomon and compelled to aid in the building of the Temple, for the demon king alone knew where to find the shamir, the wondrous worm that could cut stone without iron tools.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The pre-Islamic and Islamic folklore of the Near East was full of the jinn, beings created from smokeless fire as humans were created from clay. The jinn lived in a parallel society with their own tribes and faiths, mostly unseen but able to take many shapes. They might haunt deserts, ruins, and bathhouses, help or harm a person according to their nature, and the ifrit and the marid were named among their most powerful and fearsome kinds.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The folklore of the evil eye was deeply woven into the cultures of the Near East and the Mediterranean. It was believed that a glance of envy or admiration, even unintended, could carry a harmful power that brought sickness, accident, or ruin upon its object. Children, livestock, and new ventures were thought especially vulnerable. Blue beads, the open-palmed hamsa, recited blessings, and a pinch of salt were all used to absorb, deflect, or break the malign power of the watching eye.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Solomon, in folk tradition, was not only a wise king but a master of the spirit world. Legend held that he possessed a signet ring engraved with a divine name, and with it he could command the jinn and the demons, sealing the rebellious ones into brass vessels and casting them into the sea. The demons labored at his bidding, raising the Temple and revealing hidden knowledge, and Solomon's mastery over them became the seed of a vast later literature of magic and binding.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: Among the demons of Mesopotamian belief that fed into later Near Eastern folklore was Lamashtu, a fearsome goddess-demon who preyed on pregnant women and newborn children. She was depicted with the head of a lioness, the teeth of a donkey, and a body suckling a dog and a pig. To repel her, families placed amulets bearing the image of a rival demon, Pazuzu, whose own ugliness and ferocity were turned to protective use, set to guard the household against the worse evil that Lamashtu would bring.

subtopic: Jewish and Near Eastern folk demonology
sentence: The incantation bowls of late antique Mesopotamia are a vivid trace of Near Eastern folk demonology. These simple clay bowls were inscribed in spiraling lines of script with protective spells, often naming the demons to be bound and the angels called to drive them away, and sometimes drawn with the image of a chained demon at the center. Buried upside down beneath the threshold or the corners of a house, they were meant to trap any evil spirit that tried to enter.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Thor, the thunder god, once awoke to find his hammer Mjolnir stolen, and without it Asgard lay open to its enemies. The giant Thrym confessed he had hidden it deep in the earth and would return it only in exchange for the goddess Freyja as his bride. Freyja refused with such fury that the halls of the gods shook, and so Thor himself was dressed in a bridal veil and gown, and Loki disguised as the bridesmaid, and the two went to the giants' feast to win the hammer back by trickery.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: At Thrym's wedding feast the disguised Thor nearly gave himself away, devouring an entire ox and eight salmon and draining three barrels of mead. When the suspicious giant peered beneath the veil and recoiled from the bride's blazing eyes, Loki smoothly explained that Freyja had not slept for eight nights in her eagerness for the marriage. At last the hammer was brought out to hallow the bride, and Thor seized it, threw off his disguise, and laid every giant in the hall low.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Thor and Loki journeyed to the stronghold of the giant Utgarda-Loki, who challenged them to a series of contests. Thor was given a drinking horn and could not empty it; he wrestled an old woman and was forced to one knee; he tried to lift a gray cat and managed only to raise one paw. Afterward Utgarda-Loki revealed the truth: the horn's end was joined to the sea, the old woman was old age itself, and the cat was the Midgard Serpent. Thor's failures had been magnificent.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: When the gods needed a great wall built around Asgard, a master builder offered to raise it within a single winter, asking as payment the sun, the moon, and the goddess Freyja. The gods, on Loki's advice, agreed, certain the task was impossible. But the builder's mighty stallion hauled stone so swiftly that the wall neared completion in time. To save Freyja, Loki transformed himself into a mare and lured the stallion away, and the wall was left unfinished and the giant's price unpaid.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Tyr, the bravest of the Norse gods, gave his hand for the safety of the world. The gods sought to bind the monstrous wolf Fenrir, and the dwarves forged a fetter as soft as silk but unbreakable. Fenrir, suspecting a trick, would submit to the binding only if a god placed a hand in his jaws as a pledge of good faith. Tyr alone stepped forward and laid his right hand between the wolf's teeth. When Fenrir found himself bound and could not break free, he bit the hand off, and Tyr bore the loss without complaint.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: The poetry of the Norse was a gift won by Odin through cunning and theft. The mead of poetry, brewed from the blood of a wise being and honey, was hoarded by a giant in a mountain. Odin bored a hole into the rock, slipped through as a serpent, seduced the giant's daughter who guarded the mead, and drank all three vats dry. He escaped in the shape of an eagle, pursued by the furious giant, and spat the precious mead into vessels the gods had set out, sharing the art of poetry with the worthy.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Idunn was the goddess who kept the golden apples that preserved the youth of the gods, and when the giant Thjazi forced Loki to lure her out of Asgard, the gods began at once to wither and gray. Realizing the cause, they threatened Loki with death unless he undid his treachery. Loki borrowed Freyja's falcon cloak, flew to the giant's hall, turned Idunn into a nut, and carried her home in his talons with Thjazi raging close behind in eagle form, only to be burned to death at the walls of Asgard.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Freyja, the foremost goddess of the Vanir who came to dwell among the Aesir, was a deity of love, fertility, war, and magic. She owned the precious necklace Brisingamen, won from four dwarves, and a cloak of falcon feathers that let its wearer fly. She rode a chariot drawn by two great cats and a boar with golden bristles. Half of those slain in battle came to her hall, Folkvangr, before the other half went to Odin's Valhalla, and so Freyja shared even the harvest of the dead.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: The giant Hrungnir once boasted in Asgard that he would tear down the gods' halls and carry off their goddesses, and Thor challenged him to a duel. The giant armored himself with a shield of stone and a great whetstone for a weapon. When Thor's hammer flew, Hrungnir hurled the whetstone, and the two collided in mid-air. The hammer shattered the stone and struck the giant dead, but a fragment of the whetstone lodged in Thor's head, and he was said to carry it there ever after.

subtopic: Norse Aesir gods and their adventures
sentence: Thor went fishing with the giant Hymir and rowed far out beyond the giant's accustomed waters. Baiting his hook with the head of an ox, Thor cast into the deep and hooked the Midgard Serpent itself. He hauled with such tremendous strength that his feet broke through the bottom of the boat and braced against the seabed, and he drew the venom-spitting serpent up until its head broke the surface. But the terrified Hymir cut the line, and the great enemy of the gods sank back into the sea to await Ragnarok.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The Inuit of the Arctic coasts told of Sedna, the mother of the sea and the mistress of all its creatures. In one telling she was a woman cast from a boat by her own father, and when she clung to the side, her frozen fingers were cut away. The severed fingers sank and became the seals, the walruses, and the whales, and Sedna herself descended to rule the depths. When she is angered by human wrongdoing, she keeps the animals from the hunters, and only a shaman can travel down to comb her hair and soothe her.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The angakkuq, the Inuit shaman, was the essential intermediary between the human community and the powerful spirits of the Arctic world. In times of famine or sickness, the angakkuq would fall into a trance and send their soul on a perilous journey, perhaps down through the sea ice to the dwelling of Sedna, to plead with her for the release of the game animals. The shaman returned with knowledge of which taboo had been broken and what the people must do to set the world right again.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: Inuit tradition holds that everything in the world, the animals, the weather, the very stones, possesses an inua, an indwelling spirit or person. The seal that gave itself to the hunter had an inua that had to be honored, and so a freshly killed seal was offered a drink of fresh water to slake the thirst of its spirit. To treat the animals and the land without respect was to offend their inue, and offended spirits could withhold the game and bring the killing cold.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The Inuit told of the origin of the sun and the moon as a brother and a sister. The sister, ashamed and angered after discovering that a night visitor to her bed had been her own brother, smeared his face with soot and fled with a torch into the sky to become the sun. The brother seized a torch and pursued her, becoming the moon, but his torch burned lower, which is why the moon shines with a dimmer light, forever chasing the sun across the polar sky.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: Among the spirit-beings feared in Inuit folklore was the qalupalik, a creature of the sea that lived beneath the ice. It was said to have green skin, long hair, and long fingernails, and it carried a pouch on its back called an amautik. The qalupalik would hum near the shore and the breathing holes, waiting to snatch children who wandered too close to the dangerous ice without their parents. The legend kept the young safely back from the deadly edges of the frozen sea.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The shimmering curtains of the aurora borealis were given many meanings in Arctic spirit tradition. Some Inuit groups believed the dancing lights were the spirits of the dead, playing a game with a walrus skull as their ball. Others held that the lights could be summoned by whistling, or warned that they were dangerous and might descend to carry off a careless onlooker. The night sky over the Arctic was not empty but populated, a place where the dead moved and watched.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The tupilaq was an object of dark Inuit folk magic, a small figure secretly fashioned from animal bones, skin, and parts of a corpse, then brought to life by chants and placed into the sea. The maker sent the tupilaq to hunt down and kill an enemy. But the practice was perilous, for if the intended victim possessed greater spiritual power, they could turn the tupilaq back upon its creator, and the sorcerer would be destroyed by the very thing they had made.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: Inuit folklore was rich with tales of the ijiraq and other land spirits that haunted the tundra and could lead a traveler astray. The ijiraq was a shapeshifter, glimpsed from the corner of the eye and gone when looked at directly, and it was blamed for the disappearance of those who lost their way in the featureless snow. Some stories said the ijiraq abducted children and hid them, and that the lost child became an ijiraq in turn, neither living nor dead, wandering the frozen land forever.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: The Inuit feared the amaguq and the fearsome amarok, a giant wolf of the legends. The amarok was said to hunt alone rather than in a pack, and to prey upon those foolish or arrogant enough to hunt by night without companions. The story functioned as a warning rooted in hard Arctic reality, teaching that the safe and respectful way to live in that unforgiving land was to keep to the community and not to test the dark and the cold alone.

subtopic: Inuit and Arctic spirit traditions
sentence: Inuit tradition told of the adlet, beings born of the union of a woman and a great dog, half human and half hound. The story explained the origin of certain feared peoples and of dog-kind itself, for the woman set some of her strange children adrift in a boot or a vessel and sent the rest inland. The tale, like much Arctic folklore, used the figures of animals and spirits to explain the shape of the world, the kinds of beings in it, and the uneasy boundaries between them.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The Shahnameh, the great Persian epic completed by the poet Ferdowsi around the year 1010, recounts the legendary history of Persia from the creation of the world to the Arab conquest. It opens with the first king, Keyumars, who taught humankind to clothe themselves and prepare food. The epic weaves together myth, legend, and history into fifty thousand couplets, and it preserved the heroic traditions of pre-Islamic Iran for all the generations that followed.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The tyrant Zahhak is among the great villains of the Shahnameh. The evil spirit Ahriman, in disguise, kissed the young prince upon both shoulders, and from each spot a ravening serpent grew. The serpents could be quieted only by being fed each day with the brains of two young men, and so Zahhak's thousand-year reign became a daily slaughter. At last the blacksmith Kaveh, who had lost his own sons to the serpents, raised his leather apron upon a spear as a banner of revolt.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The greatest hero of the Shahnameh is Rostam, a warrior of immense strength who served the kings of Persia for centuries. He rode a mighty steed named Rakhsh, the only horse strong enough to bear him, and he undertook the Seven Labors, a series of trials including the slaying of a lion, a dragon, and the terrible White Demon, to rescue his king from captivity. Rostam embodied the loyal champion, his vast power always set in the service of the throne and the land.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The most heartbreaking tale of the Shahnameh is that of Rostam and his son Sohrab. The two had never met, for Rostam left the boy's mother before his birth. Sohrab grew into a mighty warrior and went seeking his famous father, but fate set them on opposite sides of a war. They fought as strangers, and Rostam dealt the younger man a mortal wound. Only as Sohrab lay dying did he reveal a token his mother had given him, and Rostam understood, too late, that he had killed his own child.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The Simurgh is a marvelous bird of Persian myth, vast and ancient, nesting in the branches of a great tree and possessed of wisdom from having seen the world destroyed and reborn many times. When the hero Zal was abandoned as an infant on a mountainside because he was born with white hair, the Simurgh found him and raised him in her nest. Ever after she remained his protector, and she gave him a feather to burn in times of dire need, that she might come to his aid.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: When Rostam's wife Rudabeh suffered through a labor that threatened to kill both her and the unborn child, Zal burned the feather of the Simurgh. The great bird appeared and instructed him in a procedure unknown to the people of that age: to cut open the mother's side, draw forth the child, and close the wound with a salve and a chant. The child delivered in this way was Rostam himself, and the Persian tradition remembered the operation by his name.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The Shahnameh tells of Jamshid, a great early king under whose rule the world enjoyed a golden age of peace, plenty, and the absence of death. Jamshid taught the crafts of weaving, building, and medicine, and divided society into its orders. But after centuries of glory, he grew proud and declared himself divine, demanding worship as a god. The divine favor, the royal glory called farr, abandoned him, and his fall opened the way for the serpent-king Zahhak to seize the world.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The hero Fereydun overthrew the tyrant Zahhak, but he did not kill him. Counseled that the time for Zahhak's death had not yet come, Fereydun instead bound the serpent-king and imprisoned him within Mount Damavand, the great peak of Iran, where he remains chained to this day. The Shahnameh holds that at the end of time Zahhak will break free and bring a final wave of evil, until a last hero rises to destroy him and close the long story of the kings.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The tale of Bijan and Manijeh is one of the romances woven through the Shahnameh. The young Persian warrior Bijan fell in love with Manijeh, daughter of the enemy king Afrasiyab, and for this he was cast into a deep pit and sealed beneath a great stone. Manijeh, disowned by her father, kept her beloved alive by passing him food through a crack. Rostam came at last in the disguise of a merchant, lifted the stone, and freed the lovers, carrying them home to Persia.

subtopic: Persian myths and the Shahnameh
sentence: The Shahnameh holds a deep current of melancholy, for it is keenly aware that all glory passes. King after king rises, rules, and falls; hero after hero performs great deeds and dies. Ferdowsi returns again and again to the turning of the wheel of fortune and the brevity of human achievement. The epic closes with the defeat of the last Persian king and the coming of a new age, and the poet, having labored thirty years, offers his vast work as a monument that he hopes will outlast empires.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The European wonder tale almost always begins with a lack or a wrong: a king with no heir, a child stolen, a princess cursed, a family in poverty. This opening misfortune sets the hero on a journey, and the tale will not close until the lack has been filled and the wrong righted. Folklorists found that beneath the endless variety of these stories lay a small and remarkably stable set of functions, a hidden grammar that gave the wonder tale its satisfying and recognizable shape.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The youngest of three is the favored hero of countless European tales, the despised or underestimated child who succeeds where the elder siblings fail. The two older brothers ride out first, scorn the small creature who asks for help, and come to grief. The youngest shares his last crust of bread with the old woman or the talking fox, and his kindness is repaid with the magic that wins the prize. The tales insist, against the order of the world, that the last shall be first.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The motif of the impossible task runs through the wonder tales of every European nation. The hero must sort a mountain of mixed grain in a single night, empty a lake with a leaking bucket, or fetch water in a sieve. The task cannot be done by ordinary means, and so it cannot be done without the gratitude of helpers, the ants who sort the seed, the birds who carry it, the magic that the hero earned by an earlier act of mercy. The task measures not strength but the worthiness to be helped.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The interdiction and its violation drive the plot of many a wonder tale. The husband may look upon any room of the castle but one; the wife may ask her mysterious bridegroom anything but his name; the girl must be home before midnight. The forbidden thing is always done, the door always opened, the question always asked. The breaking of the rule is not mere disobedience but the engine of the story, the act that plunges the hero into the trouble they must then spend the tale escaping.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The grateful animal is among the most beloved helpers of the European wonder tale. The hero, traveling toward the great task, comes upon a fish stranded out of water, an ant beneath a careless foot, an eagle caught in a snare. Where the cruel brothers would pass by or do harm, the true hero stops to help, asking nothing. Later, at the moment of greatest need, the saved creature returns, and the small mercy shown in passing turns out to have been the whole secret of the hero's success.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The false hero is a recurring villain of the wonder tale, the one who claims the credit and the reward that rightly belong to another. The true hero slays the dragon but is wounded or sleeping; an impostor finds the body, cuts off the dragon's heads, and carries them to the king to claim the princess. The tale builds to the moment of unmasking, when the real hero produces the dragon's tongues, hidden away as proof, and the false hero's lie collapses in the wedding hall.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: Magical objects pass from hand to hand through the wonder tale: the tablecloth that lays itself with a feast, the purse that never empties, the boots that stride seven leagues, the cloak that renders the wearer invisible. The objects are rarely the hero's by right; they are gifts from a grateful donor, or won by a clever trade, or stolen back from a thieving giant. Their power solves a single difficulty and is often lost again, for the wonder tale grants its marvels sparingly and never lets them last.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The number three governs the wonder tale with quiet authority. There are three brothers, three wishes, three trials, three nights of dancing, three days of grace. The first two attempts establish the pattern and usually fail; the third completes it and succeeds. The threefold repetition gave the oral storyteller a reliable scaffold, let the listener anticipate and savor the coming turn, and built the tale toward its resolution with a rhythm that feels less like a rule than like the natural breathing of the story.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The cruel stepmother stalks the European wonder tale, the figure who divides the household and drives the innocent child into the forest, the cinders, or the cooking pot. Folklorists have long suspected that she absorbed darker stories, that an earlier age told of cruel mothers and that the storytellers, unwilling to speak such a thing, displaced the cruelty onto the second wife. Whatever her origin, she became the indispensable engine of persecution that the persecuted heroine must survive and finally escape.

subtopic: Fairy tale motifs and the European wonder tale
sentence: The transformation and its breaking lie at the heart of many wonder tales. A prince is bound in the shape of a frog, a bear, a serpent, a beast; a sister is turned into a bird, a brother into a deer. The spell can be broken only by a precise and difficult act of love or loyalty, a kiss freely given, a shirt of nettles sewn in silence, a year of patient suffering. When the enchantment lifts and the true form returns, the tale affirms that beneath every monstrous shape a worthy soul was waiting to be released.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The volcano goddess Pele is the most vivid figure of Hawaiian legend, a being of fire and fierce temper who makes her home in the crater of Kilauea. Hawaiians tell that Pele can appear in many forms, sometimes as a beautiful young woman, sometimes as a frail old crone seeking a ride or a kindness. Those who treat the stranger with aloha are blessed, while those who turn her away may find their land overrun by her lava, for the goddess never forgets a discourtesy.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: Hawaiian legend tells of the menehune, a small and industrious people who lived in the forests and worked only by night. They were said to be master builders, able to complete a great fishpond, a temple, or a watercourse in a single night, working in long lines that passed the stones from hand to hand. If a task was not finished before dawn, the menehune would abandon it forever, and certain unfinished ancient structures were pointed out as proof of their interrupted labors.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The demigod Kamapuaa was a hog-man of Hawaiian legend, able to take the form of a man, a great black pig, or various plants and fish. He was Pele's rival and sometime lover, and their tempestuous affair was told as a clash of elements, the fire of the volcano against the rain and lush growth that Kamapuaa commanded. When Pele's lava threatened to consume him, Kamapuaa called down the rains and the green things, and the two divine forces fought each other to an exhausted, world-shaping stalemate.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The legend of Naupaka explains the strange flower of the Hawaiian shores, a bloom that looks as if it has been torn in half. The tale tells of two lovers separated by fate or by rank, one bound to the mountains and one to the sea. In her grief one of them tore a flower in two, keeping half and giving half to her beloved. Ever since, the naupaka of the mountains and the naupaka of the beach each bear only half a flower, and the legend says they will be whole only when the lovers are reunited.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: Hawaiian tradition speaks of the aumakua, ancestral guardian spirits that watch over a family across the generations. An aumakua might take the form of a shark, an owl, a hawk, a turtle, or another creature, and a family that recognized a shark as its aumakua would never harm one and might be protected by it in the water.
