The aumakua bridged the living and the dead, the ancestors continuing to guide and guard their descendants through the body of a chosen animal.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The night marchers, the huaka'i po, are among the most feared spirits of Hawaiian belief, the ghostly processions of ancient warriors who travel sacred paths on certain nights. They are heralded by the sound of drums and conch shells and the glow of torches, and to look upon them or to stand in their path is said to bring death. Hawaiian custom held that a person caught in the way of the night marchers should lie face down on the ground and show no disrespect, hoping a marching ancestor would claim them as kin.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The Samoan legend of the turtle and the shark tells of a blind old woman and her granddaughter, driven from their village by famine and cruelty, who threw themselves into the sea off the coast of a village called Vaitogi. Rather than drowning, they were transformed, the grandmother into a turtle and the girl into a shark. The legend holds that when the people of the village sing a certain ancient song from the cliffs, a turtle and a shark will rise together from the water in answer.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The Hawaiian goddess Hina is associated with the moon and with the craft of beating bark into kapa cloth. One legend tells that Hina grew weary of her endless labor and the demands of her family, and so she climbed up a rainbow, or simply floated upward, to make a new home on the moon. There she lives still, and the shadowy patterns visible on the moon's surface are said to be Hina and her great kapa-beating board, the goddess at her work in the quiet of the sky.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The legend of Pele and her younger sister Hiiaka is one of the great narrative cycles of Hawaiian tradition. Pele sent the loyal Hiiaka on a long and dangerous journey to fetch the handsome chief Lohiau, with whom Pele had fallen in love in a dream. Hiiaka faced monsters and trials across the islands and grew close to Lohiau herself, and when she returned, Pele's jealous fury erupted, the goddess pouring her lava upon those she suspected of betraying her.

subtopic: Hawaiian and Pacific Island legends
sentence: The mo'o were the great water lizards or dragon-spirits of Hawaiian legend, vast reptilian beings, often female, who guarded fishponds, pools, and the freshwater places of the islands. A mo'o could be a fearsome guardian or a protective family aumakua, and a pool watched by one was a place to approach with care and respect. The mo'o belonged to the deep, still water, and their presence marked the boundary between the safe human shore and the powerful, watchful world beneath the surface.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: In Yoruba tradition the supreme being Olodumare entrusted the creation of the solid earth to the orisha Obatala. He was given a snail shell of soil, a five-toed hen, and a chain by which to descend from the sky to the watery formless world below. Obatala poured out the soil, set down the hen, and the hen scratched and scattered the earth in every direction until dry land spread across the waters. So the world was made firm enough to walk upon.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Obatala, the orisha entrusted with shaping human bodies from clay, was a being of purity associated with the color white. One legend recounts that he sometimes drank palm wine while at his work, and that the bodies he shaped under its influence came out crooked or incomplete. For this reason Obatala became the special protector of those born with disabilities, who were regarded as sacred to him, and his devotees abstained from palm wine in his honor.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Esu, sometimes called Elegua, is the Yoruba orisha of the crossroads, the messenger who carries words and offerings between humans and the other orishas. He is a trickster, unpredictable and quick to take offense, and no ritual can succeed unless Esu is honored first, for he holds the keys to the paths. One famous story tells how Esu walked a road wearing a cap that was black on one side and white on the other, then set two friends quarreling over its color until their friendship was destroyed.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Ogun is the Yoruba orisha of iron, war, and the craft of the smith, a fierce and powerful figure who clears the path with his blade. The legends tell that when the orishas first came down to the bush-grown world, only Ogun possessed the iron tools to cut a way through the dense forest. For this the other orishas wished to make him their king, but Ogun, weary of bloodshed, withdrew into the mountains, and he remains a deity both essential and dangerous, the patron of all who work and fight with metal.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Shango, the orisha of thunder and lightning, was once, the legends say, a mortal king of the city of Oyo, a ruler of great power and a fearsome temper. After his reign ended in tragedy, he ascended and became the orisha of the storm. His devotees say that when lightning strikes, Shango has hurled a thunderstone to the earth, and the polished stone axes found in the soil are gathered as sacred objects, the very weapons cast down by the thunder god.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Oya is the Yoruba orisha of the wind, storms, and the river Niger, a warrior goddess and the companion of Shango. She commands the whirlwind and the lightning's gusting fury, and she stands as a guardian at the gateway between the living and the dead. The legends describe her as fierce and transformative, a force that sweeps away the old to clear ground for the new, and her devotees turn to her in times of upheaval and great change.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Yemoja is the Yoruba orisha of the river that bears her name, and in the traditions of the diaspora she became the mother of the ocean and of all the orishas. She is the patron of mothers and children and of the deep nurturing waters. One story tells that when Yemoja's waters broke, the great rivers of the world poured forth, and from her body the first orishas were born, making her the womb from which much of the divine world descended.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Oshun is the Yoruba orisha of the river, of sweet waters, love, beauty, and fertility, and one important story places her at the center of the world's survival. When the male orishas tried to organize the world without including her, every effort they made failed and the rains would not come. Only when they begged Oshun's forgiveness and honored her did the fertilizing waters return. The tale taught that the gentle, life-giving power she embodied could not be dismissed without ruin.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Orunmila is the Yoruba orisha of wisdom and divination, the one who was present at the creation and who knows the destiny laid out for every being. His knowledge is consulted through the system of Ifa, in which a trained diviner casts palm nuts or a divining chain and reads the patterns that fall. Each pattern points to a body of verses and stories, and within those narratives the seeker finds guidance, for the orishas speak through the ancient tales that Ifa preserves.

subtopic: Yoruba orishas and divine narratives
sentence: Yoruba narrative holds that every person, before being born into the world, kneels before Olodumare and chooses their ori, their inner head or destiny. Once chosen, the details of that destiny are forgotten upon birth, and life becomes the unfolding of a path the soul itself selected but cannot remember. The orishas and the practice of Ifa divination help a person live in harmony with their ori, and the tales of the gods are, in part, a long meditation on the meeting of choice, character, and fate.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The huntress Daphne wished only for the freedom of the wild woods, but the god Apollo, struck by one of Eros's arrows, pursued her with a desire she could not escape. As his footsteps closed and his breath stirred her hair, Daphne cried out to her father, the river god, to save her by destroying the beauty that had doomed her. At once a heaviness seized her limbs; bark crept over her smooth skin, her arms branched into boughs, her feet rooted, and the fleeing maiden became the laurel tree.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The sculptor Pygmalion, disdaining the women of his city, carved an ivory statue of such perfect beauty that he fell hopelessly in love with his own creation. He dressed it, spoke to it, brought it gifts, and at the festival of Aphrodite he prayed for a wife as lovely as his ivory maiden. When he returned home and kissed the cold statue, he felt the ivory soften beneath his lips, warmth spread through the limbs, and a pulse begin to beat. The goddess had granted his impossible wish, and the statue lived.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: Arachne was a weaver of such skill that she boasted she could surpass the goddess Athena herself, and she refused to credit the goddess for her gift. Athena came to her in disguise to warn her, then revealed herself, and the two set their looms for a contest. Arachne wove a tapestry so flawless, and so insolent in its mockery of the gods, that the furious Athena struck her. In pity or in punishment the goddess then sprinkled her with a bitter juice, and Arachne shrank into a spider, weaving forever.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The youth Narcissus was so beautiful that all who saw him fell in love, yet he scorned every admirer, including the nymph Echo, who wasted away for him until only her voice remained. As punishment, Narcissus was made to fall in love with his own reflection in a still pool. Unable to tear himself away from the unattainable image, unable to embrace it, he pined beside the water until he died. Where his body had lain, the gods caused a flower to grow, bending its head toward the water that had destroyed him.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: Niobe, queen of Thebes, boasted of her fourteen children and mocked the goddess Leto, who had borne only two. But Leto's two children were the divine archers Apollo and Artemis, and to avenge their mother they shot down all of Niobe's sons and daughters. The queen, shattered by grief beyond bearing, was turned to stone, yet even the stone could not stop weeping. The Greeks pointed to a weathered rock face on Mount Sipylus, marked by trickling water, as the petrified and ever-mourning Niobe.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The aged couple Baucis and Philemon lived in poverty in Phrygia, and when the gods Zeus and Hermes wandered the land in disguise seeking shelter, every wealthy house turned them away. Only Baucis and Philemon welcomed the strangers and shared their humble meal. The gods spared the pious couple from the flood that drowned their inhospitable neighbors, granted their wish to die at the same moment, and transformed them at the end of their long lives into two trees, an oak and a linden, growing forever from a single trunk.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The hunter Actaeon, while roaming the forest with his hounds, stumbled by chance upon a hidden grove where the goddess Artemis was bathing. To gaze upon the virgin goddess unclothed was an unforgivable trespass, even though Actaeon had not sought it. In her anger Artemis flung water in his face, and antlers sprouted from his brow, his neck lengthened, his body became that of a stag. His own pack of hunting dogs, no longer knowing their master, tore the transformed Actaeon to pieces.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The story of Tereus, Procne, and Philomela is among the darkest of the Greek transformations. After a chain of betrayal, mutilation, and a terrible revenge in which a mother served her own child to its father, the gods intervened to end the cycle of horror. As Tereus pursued the sisters with a drawn sword, all three were changed into birds: Tereus into a hoopoe with a crest like a helmet, Procne into a swallow, and Philomela into a nightingale, whose song the Greeks heard as an endless lament.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: Callisto was a nymph and a companion of the chaste goddess Artemis until Zeus deceived and seduced her. When her condition was discovered, she was banished from Artemis's band, and the jealous Hera transformed her into a bear. For years Callisto roamed the forest in that shape, until her own son, grown to be a hunter, came upon her and raised his spear. To prevent the unwitting matricide, Zeus swept them both into the sky, where they became the constellations of the Great Bear and the Little Bear.

subtopic: Greek metamorphosis myths
sentence: The young Hyacinthus was beloved of the god Apollo, and the two delighted in athletic games together. One day, as they took turns hurling the discus, the heavy disc that Apollo threw struck Hyacinthus a mortal blow, either by cruel chance or, some said, by the jealous breath of the wind god Zephyrus. As the youth's blood soaked the earth, Apollo, unable to save him, caused a flower to spring from the ground, marked with the lament of the grieving god, and named it the hyacinth in his memory.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The soucouyant of Caribbean folklore appears by day as a quiet old woman, but in the dark hours she sheds her wrinkled skin, hiding it in a mortar or a hollow, and flies through the night as a ball of fire. In this blazing form she enters homes through cracks and keyholes to drink the blood of the sleeping. The traditional defense was to find and salt her discarded skin, so that when she tried to return to it before dawn, the burning salt would make the skin no longer fit.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The duppy is the restless ghost of Jamaican and wider Caribbean folklore, the spirit of a dead person that lingers in the world to trouble the living. A duppy might be set upon an enemy by an obeah practitioner, or it might haunt the place of its burial of its own unquiet will. People guarded against duppies in many ways, scattering them with the smoke of certain herbs, hanging objects to confuse them, and burying the dead with care so the spirit would not feel cause to return.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: Papa Bois, the old man of the forest, is the guardian spirit of the woods in the folklore of Trinidad and Tobago. He is imagined as a wild, hairy figure, sometimes with cloven hooves or leaves growing from his body, and he watches over the wild animals and the trees. A hunter who kills too freely or treats the forest without respect may meet Papa Bois, who can confuse the path, summon the beasts, or transform the offender into an animal to teach the lesson of restraint.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: La Diablesse, the devil woman, walks the country roads of the French Caribbean by night, a beautiful figure in an old-fashioned wide-skirted dress and a broad hat that shadows her face. She is elegant and alluring, and she beckons to men traveling alone, leading them off the road and into the bush. The folklore warns that one of her feet is a cloven hoof, hidden beneath her long skirt, and the man who follows her may be lured over a cliff or lost forever in the dark forest.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: Across the Caribbean the stories of Anansi the spider survived the Middle Passage, and the trickster became a hero of the enslaved. Brother Anansi, small and weak but endlessly clever, outwitted Tiger, the powerful master of the animals, again and again. The tales carried a coded comfort and instruction, showing that strength was not everything, that the powerless could prevail through wit, patience, and a willingness to play the fool, and the stories were told around the fire as both entertainment and quiet lesson.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The douen of Trinidadian folklore are the spirits of children who died before they were baptized, and they are recognized by a haunting peculiarity: their feet are turned backward, the heels pointing forward. The douen wander the forests and call out the names of living children to lure them away into the bush, where they become lost. Mothers were careful never to shout their children's names too freely in open country, for fear a listening douen would learn a name and use it.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: Haitian folk tradition tells of the lwa, the spirits served in Vodou, who are organized into families or nanchon and act as intermediaries between humanity and the distant creator. Papa Legba stands at the crossroads and the gateway, and like Esu of the Yoruba he must be greeted first, for he opens the way between the worlds. The Gede spirits, presided over by the irreverent Baron Samedi, govern death and the cemetery, and their rites mingle mourning with bawdy laughter and a fierce embrace of life.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The Caribbean folktale often opens and closes with a formula, the storyteller calling out a cry and the listeners answering, a ritual that gathers the audience and marks the passage into the world of the tale. The teller might announce that this is not a true story, or warn that the tale itself is a lie, and end by sending the story away on a journey or claiming to have been kicked out of the events described. These framing devices made the telling itself a small performed ceremony.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: The folklore of the Caribbean is full of jumbies, a broad category of spirits, ghosts, and uncanny beings that haunt the islands. A jumbie might be the wandering dead, a malevolent forest spirit, or one of the named creatures like the soucouyant or the douen. Belief in jumbies shaped daily caution: people avoided certain trees said to be jumbie homes, kept children indoors after dark, and trusted in herbs, salt, and ritual to keep the restless and the hungry spirits at a safe distance.

subtopic: Caribbean and Afro-diasporic folklore
sentence: Cuban and Brazilian traditions descended from West African religion preserved the orishas under new names and forms, blended with Catholic saints during centuries of forced conversion. In Cuban Santeria the thunder orisha Shango was venerated alongside the image of a Christian saint, and the stories of Yemaya, Ochun, and Obatala continued to be told. The narratives survived the crossing and the suppression, hidden in plain sight, and the gods of the Yoruba kept their voices in the folklore of the Americas.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The dragon takes profoundly different forms in the world's mythologies. In the imagination of medieval Europe it was a fire-breathing reptile, a hoarder of gold and a devourer of maidens, a monster to be slain by a saint or a knight. In China the dragon was its near opposite, a benevolent serpentine being of the rains and rivers, a bringer of fortune and a symbol of imperial power. The same word came to name two creatures whose meanings were almost reversed.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The Norse hero Sigurd won his fame by slaying the dragon Fafnir, a being who had once been a dwarf or a man, transformed into a monstrous serpent by his greed for a cursed hoard of gold. On the advice of the smith Regin, Sigurd dug a pit in the path Fafnir crawled to drink, and as the great worm passed overhead he drove his sword up into its belly. He roasted the dragon's heart, and tasting its blood upon his thumb, he found he could suddenly understand the speech of birds.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The Greek imagination filled the edges of the world with serpent-monsters. The Python coiled at Delphi until Apollo slew it; the Hydra of Lerna grew two heads for each one struck off; Ladon, the hundred-headed dragon, guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides; and the dragon of Colchis, sleepless and ever-watchful, guarded the Golden Fleece until the witch Medea lulled it into sleep so that Jason could carry the prize away.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The feathered serpent is one of the great deities of Mesoamerica, known as Quetzalcoatl to the Aztecs and Kukulkan to the Maya. Unlike the monstrous dragons that heroes were sent to kill, the feathered serpent was a creator and a giver of gifts, associated with the wind, with learning, with the planet Venus, and with the priesthood. Its image, a serpent's body clothed in the brilliant plumage of the quetzal bird, joined the earthbound snake to the sky and made of the union a god.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: In Hindu mythology the cosmic serpent Shesha, also called Ananta, the endless one, is a being of many heads upon whose vast coils the god Vishnu reclines, floating on the ocean of milk between the cycles of creation. Shesha is said to hold all the planets of the universe upon his hoods and to sing the glories of the gods. When he uncoils, time moves forward and creation begins; when he coils again, the universe returns to its rest, and so the serpent measures the breathing of the cosmos.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The ouroboros, the serpent or dragon devouring its own tail, appears in the symbolic traditions of ancient Egypt, Greece, and beyond. Forming an unbroken circle, the self-consuming serpent came to signify the eternal cycle of destruction and renewal, the unity of all things, and time turning endlessly upon itself. It is found coiled around the sun god in Egyptian funerary art and threaded through later alchemical writings, a single image carrying the idea that every ending feeds a beginning.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The Japanese tale of Yamata-no-Orochi tells of an eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent so vast its body spread across eight valleys and eight hills. Each year it devoured a maiden, and when only one daughter of a grieving family remained, the storm god Susanoo came to their aid. He set out eight vats of strong rice wine; the serpent plunged a head into each and drank itself into a stupor. While it slept, Susanoo cut the monster apart, and in one of its tails he found a great sword, which became a treasure of the imperial line.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The legend of Saint George and the dragon spread across medieval Christendom and became the model of the dragon-slaying tale. A town was terrorized by a dragon that demanded its citizens as tribute, until the lot fell upon the king's own daughter. As she awaited her death, the knight George rode up, made the sign of the cross, and pierced the dragon with his lance. He led the subdued beast into the town and the people, in gratitude and awe, accepted his faith.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The rainbow serpent of Aboriginal Australian tradition is among the oldest dragon-figures imagined by any culture, a vast snake whose body shaped the rivers and gorges and whose presence brings the rain. Across the world, water and the serpent are bound together: the Chinese dragon kings rule the seas, the Hindu nagas guard rivers and treasures, and the West African Mami Wata wears her great serpent. The coiling form of the snake, like a winding river or a striking wave, made it the natural ruler of the waters in the human imagination.

subtopic: Dragons and serpents across world mythology
sentence: The Welsh national emblem, the red dragon, has its own legend. The boy Merlin was brought before a king whose tower kept collapsing, and the boy revealed the cause: beneath the foundations lay a hidden pool in which two dragons slept, one red and one white. When they were dug out, the dragons woke and fought, and Merlin prophesied that the red dragon, representing the Britons, would at last drive out the white dragon of the invaders, and the red dragon flies on the Welsh flag still.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The Tain Bo Cuailnge, the Cattle Raid of Cooley, is the central epic of the Ulster Cycle, and it begins with a quarrel in bed. Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband Ailill compared their possessions and found themselves perfectly matched, until Ailill produced a magnificent white-horned bull that had no equal in Medb's herds. To restore the balance and her pride, Medb resolved to win the great brown bull of Cooley, by purchase if she could and by war if she must.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: Cu Chulainn, the great hero of the Ulster Cycle, was born Setanta and earned his name as a boy. Invited to a feast at the house of the smith Culann, the child arrived late, and the smith's monstrous guard hound attacked him. Setanta killed the beast with his bare hands, or by driving a hurling ball down its throat. To make amends, the boy offered to guard the smith's house himself until a new hound was reared, and so he became Cu Chulainn, the Hound of Culann.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: When Medb's army marched on Ulster, the warriors of the province were laid low by a strange curse, struck down with the pangs of a woman in childbirth. Only Cu Chulainn, untouched by the curse, stood between the invaders and the heart of Ulster. He invoked the right of single combat, an ancient custom, and held the army at a ford, fighting and defeating champion after champion sent against him, one each day, while alone he bought time for his stricken people to recover.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The most agonizing episode of the Tain is the combat between Cu Chulainn and Ferdiad. The two had trained together as youths under the warrior-woman Scathach and loved one another as foster-brothers. Now Medb compelled Ferdiad to face the hero at the ford. For three days they fought and then tended each other's wounds and shared food across the water by night. On the fourth day Cu Chulainn was forced to use the dreadful barbed spear, the Gae Bolga, and Ferdiad fell, and the hero wept over the friend he had killed.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: When the battle-fury, the riastrad or warp-spasm, came upon Cu Chulainn, his body contorted into a monstrous and unrecognizable shape. His muscles bulged, one eye sank into his skull and the other started out upon his cheek, his hair stood stiff with a drop of blood at each tip, and a great spout of dark blood, the hero-light, rose from the crown of his head. In this terrible transformed state he was a danger to friend and foe alike, and after the battle the men of Ulster had to plunge him into vats of cold water to cool his rage.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The death of Cu Chulainn came when his enemies turned his own code of honor against him. They knew the hero was bound by sacred prohibitions, his geasa, and they contrived a situation where every choice broke one. Mortally wounded at last, Cu Chulainn would not fall. He bound himself upright to a standing stone so that he might die on his feet, facing his enemies, and they dared not approach until a raven settled on his shoulder and they knew at last that the Hound of Ulster was dead.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The Morrigan, the great phantom queen of Irish myth, was a goddess of war, fate, and death who hovered over the battles of the Ulster Cycle. She offered her love to Cu Chulainn, and when he refused her, she turned against him, hindering him in his combats by taking the shape of an eel, a wolf, and a heifer. At the end she appeared to him as a crow, settling upon his shoulder in his final hour, the war goddess come to mark the passing of the greatest of heroes.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The Tain ends not with the triumph of Medb but with the meeting of the bulls. After all the slaughter, the great brown bull of Cooley was carried into Connacht, and there it met Ailill's white-horned bull. The two beasts fought a tremendous battle across the whole of Ireland, and the brown bull at last killed its rival, scattering the pieces of the white bull's body across the land before staggering home to die. Both prizes were lost, and the long war had won nothing for anyone.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The Fenian Cycle gathered the tales of Fionn mac Cumhaill and his warrior band, the Fianna. As a boy, Fionn was set to cook the Salmon of Knowledge, a fish that held all the wisdom of the world for whoever first tasted it. Fionn burned his thumb on the cooking salmon and put it in his mouth to ease the pain, and so the wisdom passed to him by accident. Ever after, when Fionn needed insight, he had only to press his thumb between his teeth to know the truth.

subtopic: Irish heroic cycles and the Tain
sentence: The Fenian Cycle tells the sorrowful tale of Diarmuid and Grainne. Grainne was promised in marriage to the aging Fionn mac Cumhaill, but she loved the young warrior Diarmuid and laid him under a binding obligation to flee with her. The lovers were pursued across Ireland by the jealous Fionn for many years. When at last a reconciliation seemed near, Diarmuid was gored by an enchanted boar, and Fionn, who had the gift of healing water in his cupped hands, let the water slip away until it was too late.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: The Inca told that the creator god Viracocha rose from the depths of Lake Titicaca to make the world. He first fashioned a race of beings, but displeased with them, he destroyed them in a great flood and turned others to stone. Then Viracocha made the sun, the moon, and the stars, and a new humankind, painting each nation with its own dress and language and customs. His work done, the creator walked across the land teaching, and at last departed across the western ocean, promising one day to return.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: The founding myth of the Inca dynasty tells of Manco Capac and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo, children of the sun god, who emerged from the waters of Lake Titicaca. The sun sent them to find the place where a golden staff would sink into the earth, for there they were to build a great city. They wandered until they reached the fertile valley where the staff vanished into the rich soil, and on that spot they founded Cuzco, the navel of the Inca world.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: Another version of the Inca origin tale speaks of four brothers and four sisters who came out of a cave at a place called Pacaritambo. They set out to find good land, and along the way the brothers contended for leadership. One was sealed back inside the cave by trickery, another was turned to stone upon a sacred mountain, and the last brother, Ayar Manco, reached the valley of Cuzco and became its first ruler, while the petrified brothers remained as worshipped huacas in the landscape.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: Inti, the sun god, was the most important deity of the Inca state and the divine ancestor from whom the ruling dynasty claimed descent. The great festival of Inti Raymi was held at the winter solstice, when the sun was at its weakest and farthest, and the people gathered at Cuzco to honor Inti and beg him to return and warm the land. The Inca ruler himself, called the son of the sun, presided over the rites that were meant to renew the bond between the people and the giver of light.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: Andean tradition revered Pachamama, the earth mother, the goddess of the soil, the harvest, and fertility. She was not a distant deity but a presence in the very ground that fed the people, and farmers honored her before planting and after the harvest. The custom of the despacho, an offering of coca leaves, food, and drink given back to the earth, expressed the belief that Pachamama gave generously but expected to be thanked, and that the relationship between people and the land was one of mutual obligation.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: The Andean peoples saw the night sky as full of meaning, and among the constellations they named were not only patterns of stars but the dark spaces between them. In the band of the Milky Way they recognized dark cloud constellations, shapes outlined by the absence of stars, including a llama with its eyes, a fox, a serpent, and a toad. The celestial llama was said to descend at night to drink water from the earthly springs, keeping the world from flooding.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: Inca belief held that the world had passed through ages, and that a great pachacuti, a turning-over of time and space, could end one age and begin another. The word named both cosmic upheavals and the transformative reign of the great Inca emperor who took it as his name. The myths spoke of past worlds destroyed by flood and fire and darkness, and of the constant possibility that the order of things could be overturned and the cosmos remade.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: A widespread Andean tale tells of a llama herder who noticed his animals behaving strangely, refusing to graze and gazing up at the night sky in distress. When he questioned the llamas, they warned him that a great flood was coming to drown the world. The herder gathered his family and all the animals he could and climbed to the top of a high mountain. The waters rose almost to the peak, and when at last they receded, the herder and his charges descended to repopulate the emptied land.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: The huacas were the sacred things and places of the Andean world, and they were everywhere: a strangely shaped rock, a spring, a mountain peak, a cave, an ancestor's mummified body, a place where something marvelous had happened. Many huacas were the petrified bodies of beings from the time of origins, brothers turned to stone, ancestors fixed in the landscape. To the Andean peoples the land itself was a vast text of myth, every notable feature the trace of a sacred story.

subtopic: Andean Inca myths and origin stories
sentence: Inca tradition held that Viracocha, having finished creating the world, did not remain to rule it but walked away to the west and stepped out across the sea, traveling upon the water as upon land. The myth left open the promise of his return, and when strange bearers reached the Andes from the ocean, the old story of the returning creator god was, in some tellings, fatally remembered, the myth of homecoming colliding with the arrival of conquest.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Minotaur, a creature with the body of a man and the head of a bull, was the shameful offspring of the queen of Crete and a divine bull. King Minos confined the monster within the Labyrinth, an inescapable maze designed by the craftsman Daedalus, and fed it with youths and maidens sent as tribute from Athens. The hero Theseus volunteered among the tribute, slew the Minotaur in the heart of the maze, and found his way out by following a thread the princess Ariadne had given him.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: Medusa was once a beautiful maiden, but transformed into a monster with serpents for hair and a gaze that turned any living thing to stone. The hero Perseus was sent to claim her head, an errand meant to kill him. Armed with a mirrored shield from Athena, winged sandals, and a cap of invisibility, Perseus approached her looking only at her reflection, never directly. He struck while she slept, and from her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, born of her blood.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Sphinx sat upon a rock outside Thebes and would not let any traveler pass unless they answered her riddle, devouring all who failed: what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening. Many died until Oedipus came and gave the answer, that it was a human being, who crawls as an infant, walks upright as an adult, and leans on a staff in old age. Defeated, the Sphinx threw herself from the rock to her death, and the road to Thebes was freed.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Chimera was a fire-breathing monster with the body and head of a lion, a goat's head rising from its back, and a serpent for a tail. The hero Bellerophon was sent to kill it, a task expected to be his doom. But Bellerophon had tamed the winged horse Pegasus, and mounted upon it he could attack the Chimera from the air, beyond the reach of its flame. He fixed a lump of lead to the tip of his spear and thrust it into the monster's mouth, where its own fiery breath melted the metal and choked it.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: Between two cliffs of a narrow strait lurked two monsters, and a sailor could not avoid both. On one side was Scylla, a creature with six long necks and six ravening heads, who snatched men from the decks of passing ships. On the other was Charybdis, a vast whirlpool that swallowed the sea three times a day and could drag a whole vessel down. Odysseus, warned by Circe, steered close to Scylla, judging it better to lose six men to her jaws than the entire ship to the whirlpool.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Cyclops Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant and a son of the sea god, trapped Odysseus and his crew in his cave and began to devour them two at a time. Odysseus could not simply kill the giant, for only Polyphemus could move the great stone blocking the cave's mouth. So the hero made the Cyclops drunk, told him his name was Nobody, and drove a sharpened stake into his single eye. When the blinded giant cried that Nobody was hurting him, his neighbors heard no reason to come.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Gorgons were three sisters, monstrous and winged, with serpents writhing for hair, and Medusa alone among them was mortal. Their faces were so terrible that to look upon them turned the beholder to stone. After Perseus took Medusa's head, it kept its dreadful power even in death, and he used it as a weapon, turning his enemies to stone with the severed face. At last he gave the head to Athena, who fixed it upon her shield, the aegis, so that the terror of the Gorgon defended the goddess herself.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Harpies were winged spirits, part woman and part bird, the snatchers who carried things away on sudden gusts of wind. They tormented the blind prophet Phineus, who had been cursed so that every time food was set before him, the Harpies swooped down to seize it or to befoul it, leaving him to starve in sight of plenty. The winged sons of the North Wind, sailing with the Argonauts, at last drove the Harpies off, and Phineus, freed from the curse, repaid his rescuers with prophecy.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: Typhon was the most terrible monster of Greek myth, a being so vast that his head brushed the stars and his arms reached from east to west, with a hundred serpent-heads, eyes of fire, and a hideous chorus of voices. He rose to overthrow Zeus and the gods, and at the sight of him many of the Olympians fled. Zeus alone stood against him, hurling his thunderbolts, and after a cataclysmic struggle he crushed Typhon beneath the weight of Mount Etna, whose eruptions are the monster's smoldering rage.

subtopic: Greek monsters and the heroes who faced them
sentence: The Nemean Lion, the Erymanthian Boar, the Stymphalian Birds, and the Cretan Bull were among the monsters set against Heracles in his labors, but the strangest of his foes was the giant Antaeus. Antaeus challenged all travelers to wrestle and was invincible, for he drew renewed strength each time he touched his mother, the Earth. Heracles discovered the secret, lifted the giant clear off the ground, and held him aloft, cut off from his source of power, until the strength drained from his body.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: In the German tale of the bremen town musicians, an old donkey, a worn-out hound, a aging cat, and a rooster facing the pot all flee their cruel masters and set out together to become musicians in the town of Bremen. On the road they come upon a robbers' cottage. Stacking themselves one upon another at the window, they let out a tremendous combined racket of braying, barking, mewing, and crowing, and the terrified robbers flee into the night, leaving the four animals a warm home of their own.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The tale of Hansel and Gretel reflects the famine and hardship of old Europe in its grim opening: a poor woodcutter's family, unable to feed two children, abandons them in the forest. Lost among the trees, the children come upon a cottage built of bread and cake and sugar, the home of a cannibal witch who fattens Hansel for her oven. It is Gretel who saves them, tricking the witch into the oven she had prepared, and the children find their way home laden with the witch's treasure.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The Pied Piper of Hamelin is a German legend with an unsettling kernel of possible history. A mysterious piper in motley clothing rid the town of a plague of rats by playing a tune that drew them all into the river to drown. When the townsfolk refused to pay the agreed reward, the piper returned and played a different tune, and this time it was the children of Hamelin who followed him out of the town, never to be seen again, the legend fixing the loss to a precise date in the year 1284.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: In the tale of Rumpelstiltskin, a miller's boastful lie traps his daughter, who is locked in a room and ordered by the king to spin straw into gold or die. A strange little man appears and spins the gold for her, taking a price each time, until at last he demands her firstborn child. He offers one escape: if she can guess his name within three days, the bargain is void. Only by chance does a messenger overhear the little man singing his own name by his fire in the forest.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm, were scholars who set out in the early nineteenth century to collect the oral tales of the German-speaking lands before they were lost. They gathered stories from storytellers, friends, and family, and published their first collection in 1812. Their motives were partly nationalist and partly scholarly, a wish to preserve a folk inheritance, and their successive editions, increasingly polished for a reading audience, fixed many wandering oral tales into the forms the world now knows.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: German folklore feared the changeling and told of household sprites called kobolds, spirits that lived in homes and mines. A kobold in the house might help with chores if treated well and offered a share of food, but turn spiteful and destructive if neglected or mocked. In the mines the kobolds were blamed for the dangers of the dark tunnels and for ore that proved worthless, and from their name, the miners' word for a deceptive blue mineral eventually gave the metal cobalt its name.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The German legend of Faust tells of a learned scholar who, dissatisfied with the limits of human knowledge and pleasure, makes a pact with the devil's emissary Mephistopheles. In exchange for years of magical power, forbidden knowledge, and every worldly delight, Faust pledges his immortal soul. The legend, rooted in tales of a real wandering magician, became one of the great myths of Europe, a warning about the price of ambition and the dangerous hunger to know and possess everything.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The Lorelei is a steep rock on the bank of the Rhine, and German legend gave it an enchantress. A beautiful maiden was said to sit upon the rock, combing her golden hair and singing a song of unearthly sweetness. The boatmen who navigated the swift and narrow waters below would look up, entranced by her song and her beauty, and lose their attention to the dangerous current, and so their boats were dashed upon the rocks and the sailors drowned beneath the singing of the Lorelei.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: Germanic tradition told of the Wild Hunt, a spectral procession of huntsmen, hounds, and horses that swept through the winter sky and the storm. The hunt was led by a great figure, sometimes named as the god Wodan, sometimes as a damned soul or a legendary king. To see the Wild Hunt was an omen of catastrophe, war, plague, or one's own death, and a person caught in its path might be swept up into the chase or trampled, and so on the wild nights people stayed indoors and kept their eyes from the sky.

subtopic: Germanic folklore and the Brothers Grimm tradition
sentence: The legend of the Erlking, the elf king, was given lasting form in German poetry. The tale tells of a father riding hard through the night forest with his sick child in his arms. The boy sees and hears the Erlking calling to him, promising games and treasures and beckoning him away, while the father, who perceives nothing but wind and mist, urges his horse onward. When the rider reaches home at last, the child in his arms is dead, claimed by the spirit the father could not see.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: Shiva, the great destroyer of the Hindu trinity, performs the cosmic dance called the Tandava, and within it the universe itself rises and falls. As Nataraja, the lord of the dance, he is depicted with one foot crushing the demon of ignorance, a ring of flames around him, a drum in one hand beating the rhythm of creation, and fire in another that will consume the worlds. His dance is destruction and renewal at once, the turning of the cosmic cycle expressed as a single, perfect motion.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: When the sacred river Ganga agreed to descend from the heavens to the earth, her fall would have been so violent that it shattered the land. To save the world, Shiva stepped beneath the descending torrent and caught the river in the tangled coils of his matted hair. There the waters wound and slowed, and Ganga flowed out gently in many streams, tamed by the god, so that her life-giving waters could nourish the earth rather than destroy it.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: The myth of the elephant-headed god Ganesha tells how Parvati created a boy from the substance of her own body and set him to guard her door. When Shiva returned and the unfamiliar boy barred his way, the god in anger struck off his head. Seeing Parvati's terrible grief, Shiva promised to restore the child and sent his attendants to bring the head of the first creature they found. They returned with the head of an elephant, and so Ganesha was given new life and his beloved, distinctive form.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: The fierce goddess Kali emerged in the heat of battle against a demon who could not be killed by ordinary means, for every drop of his spilled blood that touched the ground sprang up as a new demon. Kali, dark and terrible, extended her vast tongue across the battlefield and drank up every drop of blood before it could fall, and so the multiplying demon was at last destroyed. Lost in the frenzy of her victory dance, Kali threatened to destroy the world until Shiva lay down in her path to halt her.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: The marriage of Shiva and Parvati is one of the great love stories of Hindu myth. Parvati, determined to win the ascetic god who sat in deep meditation indifferent to the world, undertook severe austerities of her own, enduring heat and cold and hunger to match his discipline. Moved at last by her devotion and the depth of her practice, Shiva opened his eyes, recognized her as his eternal consort, and the union of the great ascetic and the mountain goddess restored balance to the cosmos.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: A famous myth explains why Shiva is called the blue-throated one. During the churning of the ocean of milk, the first thing to rise from the depths was not the nectar of immortality but a poison of such terrible potency that it threatened to destroy all creation. The gods and demons fled in terror. Shiva alone stepped forward, gathered the poison, and drank it down to save the worlds, holding it in his throat, where it stained his skin a deep and lasting blue.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: Shiva is often worshipped not in human form but as the lingam, an abstract pillar set in a circular base, an aniconic symbol of the god's generative and cosmic power. One myth recounts that Brahma and Vishnu once argued over which of them was supreme, and a column of infinite fire blazed up before them. Brahma flew upward and Vishnu dove downward, each trying to find an end to it, and both failed, for the pillar of light was Shiva himself, without beginning or end.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: The third eye of Shiva, set in the middle of his forehead, is the eye of wisdom and of destructive power. When the god of desire, Kamadeva, shot an arrow of love at Shiva to rouse him from meditation, the disturbed god opened his third eye, and a blaze of fire shot forth and burned Kamadeva to ashes on the spot. Only at the pleading of the gods and of Kama's grieving wife did Shiva later relent, allowing the god of desire to live on, though without a body.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: Shiva dwells in the high Himalayas upon Mount Kailash, the cosmic mountain, seated in eternal meditation, his body smeared with ash, a crescent moon in his hair and a serpent coiled at his neck. He is the supreme ascetic, the master of yoga, withdrawn from the world in profound stillness. Yet he is also the householder married to Parvati and the wild dancer of the Tandava, and the Hindu imagination held these opposites together, the perfect renouncer who is also the source of all life and motion.

subtopic: Hindu deities and the cosmic tales of Shiva
sentence: Hindu cosmology measures time in vast cycles called yugas and kalpas, and Shiva's role as destroyer belongs to this immense rhythm. At the end of a great cosmic age, when the world has run its course, Shiva dances the dance of dissolution and the universe is unmade, drawn back into the unmanifest. After a period of rest, creation begins anew. Destruction in this vision is not an evil but a necessary phase, the clearing away that makes the next creation possible, and Shiva presides over it as a sacred function.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Vietnamese tradition traces the origin of the people to a union of a dragon and a fairy. The dragon lord Lac Long Quan, a being of the water, married the mountain fairy Au Co, and she bore a sac containing one hundred eggs, from which one hundred children hatched. Because the dragon belonged to the lowlands and the sea and the fairy to the highlands, the parents parted, each taking fifty children, and from these children descended the Vietnamese people, the offspring of dragon and immortal.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Indonesian and Malay folklore tell of Nyai Roro Kidul, the Queen of the Southern Sea, a powerful and beautiful spirit who rules the waters off the coast of Java. Legend holds that she was once a princess of great beauty who, cursed or betrayed, threw herself into the sea and became its eternal queen. She is associated with the color green, and tradition warns swimmers along the southern shore never to wear green, lest the queen claim them and draw them down into her ocean kingdom.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: The Thai and Khmer imagination peopled the mythical Himavanta forest, the realm surrounding the sacred mountain, with countless marvelous creatures. Among them were the kinnari, half woman and half bird, gentle beings famed for their song and dance, and the naga, the great serpents who guarded treasures and the waters. The legend of Manora the kinnari, captured by a hunter and won by a prince, only to flee back to her bird-people, became a beloved tale across the region.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Philippine mythology before colonization told of a sky world ruled by powerful deities. In one widespread creation account, the supreme being Bathala made the first man and woman from a length of bamboo that split open when a great bird, weary and seeking a place to land, pecked at it. From the splitting bamboo stepped the first human pair, and from them all the peoples of the islands descended, born from a hollow stalk cracked by a tired bird.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Philippine folklore feared the aswang, a shapeshifting monster that lived as an ordinary villager by day and became a predator by night. The aswang was said to take the form of a great bird or a dog and to hunt the sick, the dying, and especially pregnant women, lapping at them with a long thread-like tongue. The folklore prescribed many defenses, from garlic and salt to holy objects, and a suspected aswang could supposedly be recognized because their reflection in the eyes appeared inverted.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Balinese tradition tells of the eternal conflict between Barong and Rangda. Barong is a benevolent lion-like creature, the king of the spirits and the protector of village and order, while Rangda is the demon queen of witches, a fearsome figure of chaos and death. In the masked dance-drama that enacts their struggle, neither truly defeats the other, for the performance affirms the unending balance between good and evil, order and disorder, that the Balinese understood to govern the world.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: The Khmer civilization wove the Hindu myth of the churning of the ocean of milk into the very stone of its temples, and the great gallery at Angkor Wat depicts gods and demons pulling the serpent-rope to win the nectar of immortality. The naga, the many-headed serpent, became a central figure of Cambodian legend, and a foundation myth told that the Khmer royal line descended from the marriage of a foreign prince and a naga princess, daughter of the serpent king who ruled the land beneath the waters.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: Burmese tradition reveres the nats, a host of spirits venerated alongside the dominant religion. Many of the most important nats are the spirits of real people who died violent or tragic deaths and whose restless power had to be honored and contained. The thirty-seven great nats each have their own legend of a life cut short by execution, accident, or grief, and shrines to them stand in homes and at sacred sites, the spirits propitiated with offerings so that their lingering power protects rather than harms.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: The folklore of Southeast Asia is haunted by the penanggalan, a horror of Malay and regional tradition. By day she is an ordinary woman, often a midwife or one who practices dark arts, but by night her head detaches from her body and floats away, trailing its entrails beneath it, glowing faintly as it drifts in search of blood. She is especially feared by women in childbirth, and households placed thorny leaves around the windows and the home to snare her dangling viscera and keep her out.

subtopic: Southeast Asian myths and legendary figures
sentence: The Ramayana traveled across Southeast Asia and was reshaped by every culture it reached. In Thailand it became the Ramakien, the national epic, with Rama as the model of righteous kingship and the demon Tosakanth in the role of Ravana. In Indonesia and Malaysia it was performed in the shadow-puppet theater, the wayang kulit, where intricately carved leather figures cast their stories upon a lit screen through the night, and the heroes and demons of an ancient Indian tale became wholly local possessions.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: Toltec legend told of a ruler-priest named Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, who governed the great city of Tula in a golden age of art and abundance. He forbade human sacrifice, asking only the offering of snakes, butterflies, and birds, and under his rule the Toltecs grew skilled in every craft. But the dark god Tezcatlipoca, his eternal rival, was determined to bring him down, and the legend of the priest-king's fall became one of the central stories of central Mexico.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: Tezcatlipoca, the smoking mirror, plotted the downfall of the virtuous Quetzalcoatl with cunning rather than force. Disguised as an old man, he visited the priest-king and offered him a drink of pulque, the fermented agave wine. Quetzalcoatl, who lived in strict purity, drank and grew drunk, and in his intoxication he disgraced himself, breaking the discipline that had been the source of his holiness. Shamed beyond bearing by what he had done, the priest-king resolved to leave his city forever.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: After his fall and shame, Quetzalcoatl departed from Tula and journeyed eastward toward the sea, leaving signs of his sorrow across the land. At the shore, the legends tell, he either set himself upon a raft of serpents and sailed away across the eastern ocean, or cast himself onto a funeral pyre, from which his heart rose into the sky to become the morning star, the planet Venus. Either way he vowed that one day he would return to reclaim his city and his throne.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: The Aztecs, who rose long after the fall of Tula, looked back on the Toltecs as a near-mythical people of unmatched skill and wisdom, and the very word Toltec became a term for a master craftsman. Aztec rulers claimed Toltec descent to legitimize their power, and they took the legend of Quetzalcoatl into their own pantheon. The feathered serpent became both an ancient priest-king of memory and a living god of wind and learning, history and myth braided together beyond unraveling.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: One of the most important deeds attributed to Quetzalcoatl was the gift of maize to humankind. The legend tells that the precious grain was hidden away inside a mountain, locked beyond the reach of the gods and of people. Quetzalcoatl, taking the form of a black ant, followed a red ant into the heart of the mountain and carried the maize kernels out grain by grain. By his cunning and his patient labor in the shape of an insect, the staple food of Mesoamerica was given to the world.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: The legend of Quetzalcoatl's promised return cast a long shadow over the history of Mexico. The Aztecs held that the feathered serpent would come back from the east in a particular year of their calendar, and the priest-king's prophecy of return was woven deeply into their sense of time and fate. When ships appeared from the eastern sea, some accounts say, the old legend stirred uneasily, and the myth of the homecoming god became entangled with the catastrophe of conquest.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: Quetzalcoatl wore many aspects in Mesoamerican belief. As Ehecatl, the wind god, he wore a curved beak-like mask through which the wind blew, and his round temples were built without corners so the wind could circle them freely. As the feathered serpent he joined earth and sky. As the morning star he was the herald of the dawn. And in the priestly legend he was the gentle king of Tula, so that a single figure held together the wind, the planet Venus, and the lost golden age.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: The Toltec legends told of the marvels of Tula in its glory, where, it was said, the cotton grew already colored in the fields, the ears of maize were as large as a man, and the gourds were so vast a person could not encircle one with their arms. The Toltec craftsmen could shape gold and feathers and stone into wonders, and their wisdom encompassed the calendar and the stars. This remembered paradise, presided over by Quetzalcoatl, was the golden age against which all later ages were measured and found wanting.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: After the death and self-immolation of Quetzalcoatl, the legend recounts, his heart was carried into the sky to become the planet Venus, but the story did not end there. The feathered serpent was said to descend afterward into the underworld, the realm of Mictlan, and to spend days among the dead before rising again as the morning star. The cycle of disappearance and return mirrored the movement of Venus itself, vanishing from the sky and reappearing, the planet's rhythm written into the myth.

subtopic: Aztec Quetzalcoatl and Toltec legends
sentence: The fall of Tula was remembered as a catastrophe brought on by the trickery of Tezcatlipoca and the departure of its priest-king. The legends told of sorcery and bad omens descending on the city, of a great famine, of dancers led to their deaths by a disguised god. With Quetzalcoatl gone into exile, the golden age ended, the Toltecs scattered, and the wondrous city was abandoned. The legend gave the Aztecs a model for the rise and inevitable fall of every civilization, including, they feared, their own.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: The jotnar, the giants of Norse myth, were the great adversaries of the gods, yet the relationship between them was tangled and intimate. The gods themselves were descended from giants, and many of them took giant lovers and giant wives. Odin's mother was a giantess, Thor's mother was the earth giantess Jord, and Loki was wholly of giant blood, accepted among the Aesir. The line between god and giant was not a wall but a porous and constantly crossed boundary.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: Loki fathered three monstrous children upon the giantess Angrboda, and when the gods learned of them and the prophecies of doom that surrounded them, they resolved to act. They cast the great serpent Jormungandr into the ocean encircling the world, where it grew until it could bite its own tail. They flung the death-goddess Hel down into the underworld to rule the dishonored dead. And the wolf Fenrir they kept among themselves, trying to bind him, until the danger forced a crueler measure.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: Hel, the daughter of Loki, was given dominion over the realm of the dead that bore her name, the destination of those who died of sickness and old age rather than in battle. She was a being half living and half corpse, one side of her body the flesh of a woman and the other the blue-black of a rotting body. In her cold hall she received the great mass of the dead, and when the gods sent a messenger to beg for the release of beloved Baldr, it was Hel who set the impossible condition for his return.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: The wolf Fenrir grew so swiftly and so vast that the gods feared him, and they resolved to bind him. He broke the first two fetters with ease, scornful of the test. So the gods commissioned the dwarves to forge a third, Gleipnir, fashioned from impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the breath of a fish. It was soft as a silken ribbon, yet the great wolf could not break it, and bound he would remain until Ragnarok.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: Loki's strangest child was Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse and the finest steed in all the worlds, who carried Odin himself. When a giant builder threatened to win an unfair bargain by completing Asgard's wall too soon with the help of his powerful stallion, Loki transformed into a mare and lured the stallion away into the forest. From that union Loki later bore a foal, the gray eight-legged Sleipnir, and gave the wondrous horse to Odin, who could ride it across the sky and down into the land of the dead.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: The frost giants of Jotunheim were ancient enemies of Thor, and the thunder god spent much of his strength upon their destruction. Yet not all of the jotnar were hostile. The giant Aegir brewed ale for the gods and hosted their feasts in his hall beneath the sea, and his wife Ran gathered the drowned into her net. The wise giant Mimir guarded a well of wisdom, and Odin sacrificed an eye to drink from it, a reminder that the giants held knowledge the gods needed.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: Skadi was a giantess who came armed to Asgard to demand vengeance for the death of her father at the hands of the gods. To make peace, the gods offered her a husband, but with a strange condition: she must choose among them by looking only at their feet. Skadi, hoping to wed the beautiful Baldr, chose the most handsome pair of feet, but they belonged to the sea god Njord. The marriage of the mountain-loving giantess and the shore-loving god could not last, and the two soon parted to their separate homes.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: Loki's role among the gods grew darker over time, from a mischievous troublemaker to the engineer of the worst catastrophe. It was Loki who guided the blind god Hodr's hand to throw the fatal mistletoe at Baldr, and Loki who, disguised as a giantess, refused to weep for Baldr and so kept him in the realm of the dead. For these crimes the gods bound Loki beneath the earth with the entrails of his own son, a venomous serpent dripping above his face until the day he would break free at Ragnarok.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: When Loki lay bound beneath the earth as punishment for the death of Baldr, his faithful wife Sigyn stayed beside him. A venomous serpent had been fastened above his face, and its poison dripped down without ceasing. Sigyn held a bowl over her husband to catch the venom, sparing him the pain. But when the bowl filled and she had to turn away to empty it, the poison fell upon Loki's face, and his agonized writhing, the Norse said, was the cause of earthquakes.

subtopic: Norse giants jotnar and Loki's children
sentence: The giant Thrym, the giant builder of the wall, the giant Hrungnir, the giant Geirrod, and the giant Utgarda-Loki all measured themselves against the gods, and all were brought low. Yet the jotnar were not simply monsters; they were an older order, the children of primal chaos who had existed before Asgard was built. The Norse cosmos was a story of the gods imposing their fragile order upon a world that the giants represented, a world always pressing back, always threatening to reclaim its own.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: Eros, the god of love himself, fell in love with the mortal princess Psyche, whose beauty rivaled that of Aphrodite. He carried her to a hidden palace and visited her only in the dark, forbidding her to look upon his face. Tormented by her jealous sisters into doubting her unseen husband, Psyche lit a lamp one night and gazed on the sleeping god. A drop of hot oil woke him, and Eros fled, leaving Psyche to wander the earth and beg Aphrodite for the chance to win him back.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: Aphrodite, furious that a mortal had captured her son and her reputation for beauty, set Psyche a series of cruel and impossible tasks. Psyche had to sort a mountain of mixed grain, gather golden wool from savage sheep, and fill a flask from a deadly waterfall. She survived each through the pity of helpers, the ants, a reed, an eagle. Her final task was to descend into the underworld itself, and her endurance through all of it at last softened the gods, who granted her immortality and reunited her with Eros.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The young lovers Pyramus and Thisbe lived in neighboring houses in Babylon, forbidden by their families to marry, and they whispered their love through a crack in the shared wall. They agreed to meet at night beneath a mulberry tree. Thisbe arrived first, but fled from a lioness, dropping her veil, which the beast tore with bloodied jaws. Pyramus, finding the bloody veil, believed Thisbe dead and killed himself; Thisbe, returning, found his body and followed him into death, and the mulberries have been dark ever since.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The dawn goddess Eos fell in love with the mortal Tithonus and begged Zeus to grant her beloved immortality, so that she would never have to lose him. Zeus granted the wish, but Eos in her haste had forgotten to ask also for eternal youth. And so Tithonus could not die, but he grew older and older, withering and shrinking, his voice thinning to an endless babble, until at last, the myth says, he was transformed into a cicada, chirping forever, an immortal trapped in unending decay.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The river god Alpheus fell in love with the nymph Arethusa, a follower of the chaste Artemis, and pursued her relentlessly. To save her, Artemis transformed Arethusa into a stream, but Alpheus, undeterred, mingled his own waters with hers. The myth held that the stream of Arethusa traveled in secret beneath the sea all the way from Greece to the island of Sicily, where it surfaced as a freshwater spring, and that the waters of the river Alpheus still followed her even there.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: Apollo's loves were marked by loss. He loved Daphne, and she became a laurel tree to escape him. He loved the youth Hyacinthus, and a discus killed him. He loved the princess Coronis, and discovered her unfaithfulness through a white raven that had spied for him; in his grief and rage he killed her, then in fury scorched the raven black, and that, the Greeks said, is why ravens are no longer white. The bright god of poetry and prophecy was, again and again, unlucky in love.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The hero Admetus was granted by the Fates a singular mercy: he could escape his appointed day of death if he could find another willing to die in his place. He asked his aged parents, and they refused, clinging to their few remaining years. Only his wife Alcestis loved him enough to consent, and she lay down and died for him. But Heracles, a guest in the grieving house, wrestled Death himself at the tomb and won, bringing Alcestis back from the grave to her astonished husband.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: Zeus pursued the mortal princess Semele and visited her in secret, and she conceived a child. The jealous Hera, disguised, planted a doubt in Semele's mind, and the princess begged her divine lover to show himself in his true form. Bound by an oath, Zeus reluctantly appeared in his full glory, and the blaze of his divinity consumed the mortal Semele utterly. But Zeus snatched the unborn child from the flames and sewed him into his own thigh, and from there was born the god Dionysus.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: The musician Orpheus, who had lost his wife Eurydice twice to the underworld, never loved again, and his grief turned him away from all women. The frenzied followers of Dionysus, the Maenads, took offense at his rejection and his sorrow, and in their wild rage they fell upon him and tore him apart. His severed head, still singing, floated down the river to the sea, and the Muses gathered the scattered pieces of the poet and buried them, while his lyre was set among the stars.

subtopic: Greek divine love and tragic romance
sentence: Ceyx and Alcyone were a devoted married couple, and when Ceyx drowned at sea, Alcyone's grief was so absolute that she threw herself into the waves to join him. The gods, moved by the depth of their love, took pity and transformed them both into kingfishers, so that they could be together upon the water that had parted them. Each winter, the Greeks said, the seas grow calm for a stretch of days so that the kingfishers can nest, the halcyon days named for Alcyone's transformed and faithful love.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: The Volsung line was descended from Odin himself, and its doom was set in motion when the god Loki, to settle a debt, took a hoard of gold from the dwarf Andvari. The dwarf, robbed even of his last ring, laid a curse upon the treasure: that it would bring ruin and death to every owner. The cursed gold passed into the keeping of a man whose son Fafnir murdered him for it and, transformed by greed, became a dragon to brood upon the hoard.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: Sigurd, the greatest hero of the Volsung line, was fostered by the smith Regin, who was the brother of the dragon Fafnir and coveted the cursed hoard. Regin reforged the shattered fragments of the great sword Gram, the blade of Sigurd's father, and the new sword was so keen it could cleave an anvil and slice a tuft of wool drifting down a stream. Armed with Gram, Sigurd rode out to do what Regin urged: to slay the dragon and win the gold.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: After slaying Fafnir, Sigurd roasted the dragon's heart over a fire at Regin's bidding. Testing whether the meat was done, he touched it and burned his thumb, and thrust it into his mouth to ease the pain. The taste of the dragon's blood granted him sudden understanding of the language of birds, and the birds in the branches above warned him that Regin meant to betray and kill him. Forewarned, Sigurd struck first, and so the smith perished by the same greed that had doomed his brother.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: Riding on from the dragon's lair, Sigurd came to a mountain ringed with a wall of flame. Within, he found a sleeping warrior in full armor, and when he cut the armor away, he discovered a woman, the valkyrie Brynhild, whom Odin had pierced with a sleep-thorn and surrounded with fire for disobeying him. Brynhild could be wakened only by a man who knew no fear, and Sigurd, who feared nothing, woke her. They pledged their love, and he gave her a ring from the cursed hoard.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: The curse of the gold worked its ruin through deception. At the court of the Burgundians, Sigurd was given a potion of forgetfulness, and his memory of Brynhild was wiped away. He married the princess Gudrun, and then, not knowing what he did, he used a shape-shifting spell to pass through Brynhild's wall of fire in the guise of another man, so that she would marry that man instead. By this magic Sigurd unknowingly betrayed the woman he had loved, and the seeds of catastrophe were sown.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: Brynhild learned at last that it had been Sigurd, not her husband, who had ridden through the flames to win her, and that he had forgotten her by sorcery and given her to another. Her love curdled into a grief and a rage beyond consolation. She demanded Sigurd's death, and goaded the Burgundian brothers until they murdered the hero in his bed, or in some tellings in the forest. Sigurd died still loving Gudrun, and never understanding the full shape of the doom that had taken him.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: When Sigurd lay dead, Brynhild's vengeance turned at last upon herself. Having brought about the death of the only man she had ever truly loved, she found no satisfaction in it, only a grief that could not be borne. She ordered a great funeral pyre prepared, and she lay down upon it beside the body of Sigurd, and was consumed in the flames with him. In death she was joined to the hero that fate, magic, and the cursed gold had kept from her in life.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: The widowed Gudrun's suffering did not end with Sigurd. She was later married, against her will, to Atli, the king of the Huns, who coveted the cursed hoard of the Volsungs. Atli treacherously invited Gudrun's brothers to his court and murdered them when they would not reveal where the gold was hidden. Gudrun, in a vengeance as terrible as the crime, killed the sons she had borne to Atli, served them to him at a feast, and then set fire to his hall, ending the long bloody saga of the cursed gold.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: The saga of the Volsungs gave the Germanic world one of its most enduring stories, and it survived in many forms. The same essential tale of the dragon-slayer, the cursed treasure, the betrayed valkyrie, and the doomed royal house appears in the German Nibelungenlied, where the hero is called Siegfried. The story carried the old conviction that fate is inescapable, that a curse once spoken runs its course, and that even the bravest hero is only a thread in a pattern already woven.

subtopic: Norse Odyssey of Sigurd and the Volsungs
sentence: Before Sigurd, the Volsung saga told of his ancestors and the strange workings of Odin's favor and disfavor upon the line. Sigmund, Sigurd's father, was the one chosen to draw a sword that Odin, appearing as a one-eyed stranger, had thrust into the trunk of a great tree growing through a hall. None could move it but Sigmund. Yet Odin who gave the sword also took it back, shattering it with his spear in Sigmund's last battle, and the broken pieces were saved for the son not yet born.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong, was born from a magical stone egg upon a mountain, and he emerged as a stone monkey full of mischief and ambition. He became the king of the monkeys, and dissatisfied with a mortal life, he sought out a Taoist master to learn the arts of immortality.
