He mastered seventy-two transformations, the ability to travel a hundred and eight thousand li in a single somersault, and a host of other powers, and his arrogance grew with his strength.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: Sun Wukong descended into the underworld and struck his own name and the names of all the monkeys from the registers of the dead, declaring himself beyond death. He stormed into the dragon king's undersea palace and demanded a weapon, taking a great iron pillar that had been used to measure the depths of the sea, which obeyed his will and could shrink to the size of a needle to be tucked behind his ear. Heaven could no longer ignore the rampaging stone monkey.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: To pacify Sun Wukong, the Jade Emperor invited him to heaven and gave him a meaningless minor post as keeper of the heavenly horses. When the Monkey King discovered he had been mocked, he rebelled, declaring himself the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. He raided the peaches of immortality, devoured the pills of the elixir, and fought off every army heaven sent against him, until at last the celestial host could not contain the chaos that one stone monkey had unleashed.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: Only the Buddha himself could subdue the Monkey King. He challenged Sun Wukong to leap out of the palm of his hand, and the confident monkey somersaulted to the edge of the universe, where he found five great pillars and marked one to prove he had been there. Returning in triumph, he learned that the five pillars had been the Buddha's fingers; he had never left the palm. The Buddha closed his hand into a mountain and imprisoned the Great Sage beneath it for five hundred years.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: After five hundred years beneath the mountain, Sun Wukong was released to serve as the protector of the monk Xuanzang on his pilgrimage to the west to fetch the sacred scriptures. To keep the unruly monkey obedient, the bodhisattva Guanyin placed a golden band around his head, and whenever the monk recited a certain spell, the band would tighten and cause Sun Wukong unbearable pain. Thus the most powerful being in the tale was bound to humility by a circle of metal and a few spoken words.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: The pilgrimage to the west gathered a strange company around the monk Xuanzang. Besides the Monkey King there was Zhu Bajie, the pig-spirit, a gluttonous and lustful figure expelled from heaven and reborn in a pig's body. There was Sha Wujing, the sand monk, a former heavenly general doing penance in a river. And there was the dragon prince transformed into the white horse that carried Xuanzang. Together this band of reformed monsters and a gentle monk journeyed through eighty-one ordeals.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: The pilgrims faced eighty-one calamities on the road to the west, for the journey had to be hard if the scriptures were to be earned. They met demons who wished to eat the flesh of the holy monk to gain immortality, kingdoms ruled by sorcerers, mountains of fire, and rivers that could not be crossed. Again and again Sun Wukong used his cunning and his transformations to defeat the monsters, sometimes calling upon the gods of heaven for aid, and the company moved on toward their distant goal.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: One of the most famous episodes of the pilgrimage was the battle against the Princess Iron Fan, who possessed a magic fan that could raise hurricane winds. The pilgrims needed the fan to quench the Flaming Mountains that blocked their road. Sun Wukong tried trickery, transforming himself into a tiny insect to be swallowed and then tormenting her from within, and into the shape of her own husband, the Bull Demon King, in a long contest of shapeshifting and deception to win the fan.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: At the end of the long journey, the pilgrims reached the Buddha's paradise in the west and received the sacred scriptures, and for their faithfulness through eighty-one ordeals each was rewarded. The monk Xuanzang and the Monkey King were both elevated to the rank of Buddha; the pig and the sand monk were given holy posts; the dragon-horse became a true dragon again. The golden band that had bound Sun Wukong to obedience vanished from his head, for he no longer needed it.

subtopic: Chinese Journey to the West and Monkey King
sentence: The Monkey King became one of the most beloved figures in all of Chinese folklore, his story endlessly retold in opera, painting, and tale. He embodied a delightful contradiction: a rebel who defied heaven itself, yet who was ultimately redeemed through discipline and service. Audiences cheered his irreverence and his cunning, his refusal to accept his place, even as the tale wrapped his wild energy within a journey toward wisdom, and the irrepressible stone monkey remained a hero for the powerless and the bold.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The myth of Osiris was, at its heart, a story of the agricultural year. When the god was slain and dismembered and then revived by Isis, the Egyptians saw the death and rebirth of the land itself. Osiris became associated with the grain, and small clay beds shaped in his image were planted with seeds and watered, so that the sprouting green of the growing barley was the resurrected god rising from his own buried body, the harvest a yearly proof that life returns from death.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The Mesopotamian myth of Inanna's descent into the underworld and the substitution of her husband Dumuzi explained the cycle of the seasons. Dumuzi was a shepherd god of fertility, and his fate was to spend half the year imprisoned among the dead while his sister took his place for the other half. His descent was the withering of the land in the dry season, and his return was the renewal of growth, the god's movement between the worlds keeping time with the turning year.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The annual flooding of the Nile, which spread fertile black silt across the fields, was woven into Egyptian myth. The flood was sometimes said to be caused by the tears of Isis, weeping for her murdered husband Osiris, so that the goddess's grief became the source of the land's abundance. The star Sirius, rising at dawn just before the flood season, was identified with Isis, and its reappearance in the sky was the signal that the life-giving inundation was near.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The Levantine myth of Baal, the storm god who brought the rains, told of his struggle against Mot, the god of death and the parched dry season. Mot swallowed Baal, and the storm god descended into the underworld, and without him the rains failed and the earth cracked and withered. Baal's sister, the fierce goddess Anat, hunted down Mot and destroyed him, grinding him like grain, and Baal returned to life, the rains came again, and the fertility of the land was restored.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The Phrygian myth of Cybele and her young consort Attis was a tale of death, mourning, and renewal tied to the spring. Attis, a god of vegetation, died beneath a pine tree, and from his blood violets were said to spring. His cult mourned his death in early spring and then celebrated his return, and the pine tree, cut and carried in procession, became the symbol of the god whose dying and rising matched the bare winter and the greening of the new season.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The myth of Adonis, beloved of Aphrodite and adopted from Near Eastern tradition, told of a beautiful youth killed by a wild boar, from whose blood the red anemone flower sprang. After his death, a compromise among the gods allowed Adonis to spend part of the year in the underworld and part in the world above. Women planted shallow gardens of fast-growing, fast-withering seeds in his honor, and the quick blooming and swift death of these Adonis gardens enacted the fragile cycle of vegetation.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The sacred marriage, the hieros gamos, was a ritual and mythic theme across the ancient Near East. In Mesopotamia the union of the goddess Inanna and the shepherd Dumuzi, often enacted by a priestess and the king, was believed to ensure the fertility of the land, the flocks, and the people for the coming year. The myth of the divine lovers and the rite that mirrored it bound the prosperity of the whole community to the symbolic coupling of the powers of fertility.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The Egyptian goddess Hathor was a deity of love, music, joy, and fertility, often depicted as a cow or as a woman with cow's horns cradling the sun disc. She was the nurturing mother who suckled the pharaoh and the goddess who welcomed the dead. As the bringer of fertility she was honored at festivals of drinking and dancing, and her gentle aspect was understood to be the calmed and benevolent form of the same divine power that, as the lioness Sekhmet, could bring devastation.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: The god Min was one of the most ancient deities of Egypt, a god of male fertility, generation, and the harvest. At the festival held in his honor at the start of the harvest season, the pharaoh himself took part in the rites, and a sheaf of grain was ceremonially cut in the god's presence. Min was also a protector of the desert routes and the mining expeditions, but his central role was as the embodiment of the generative force that renewed the crops, the herds, and the royal line.

subtopic: Egyptian and Near Eastern fertility cycles
sentence: Across the ancient Near East, the recurring myth of the dying and returning god gave a sacred shape to the fear and hope of agricultural life. Osiris, Dumuzi, Baal, Attis, Adonis: each was a deity bound to the grain or the rain, each suffered death or descent, and each was mourned and then welcomed back. Behind the variety of names lay a single deep pattern, the human need to believe that the brown death of the dry season and the winter was not final, and that green life would always come again.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: An old African folktale tells how the tortoise won a race against the swift hare or the antelope, not through cunning trickery but through a clever cooperation. The tortoise gathered all his kinfolk, who looked alike, and stationed one at each marker along the racecourse. Whenever the boastful runner called out to taunt the tortoise, a tortoise was always there ahead to answer, and the exhausted, baffled runner finally collapsed, certain he could never overtake so swift a creature.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A widespread African tale explains why the tortoise has a cracked and patchworked shell. The tortoise wished to join the birds at a great feast in the sky and persuaded each bird to give him a feather so he could fly. At the feast he tricked the birds out of all the food by claiming a false name meant everything was for him. In their anger the birds took back their feathers, and the tortoise had to fall to earth. He asked the animals to pile up soft things, but landed on hard objects and shattered his shell.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale told across many African communities recounts a contest among the animals to see who is truly the wisest or the strongest, and the answer overturns the expected order. The mighty elephant and the fierce lion are humbled, and it is some small or unregarded creature, the tortoise, the hare, the spider, who proves that intelligence and patience outmatch raw power. The tales delighted listeners by toppling the proud and rewarding the clever underdog.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: An East African tale tells why the bat flies only at night. In an ancient war between the beasts of the land and the birds of the air, the bat refused to commit to either side. When the birds seemed to be winning, the bat showed its wings and claimed to be a bird; when the beasts gained the upper hand, it showed its teeth and furred body and claimed to be a beast. When peace came, both sides recognized the bat's treachery and cast it out, and so the ashamed bat hides by day and ventures forth only in the dark.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale from West Africa tells why the sky is far from the earth. Long ago the sky hung low, and people could simply break off a piece of it to eat, for the sky itself was food. But the people grew wasteful and greedy, breaking off far more than they could eat and throwing the rest away. The sky, offended by the waste of its generous gift, rose higher and higher out of reach, and from that day people had to labor in the fields for their bread.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A well-known African tale explains why the sun and the moon live in the sky. In the beginning the sun and the water were great friends, but the sun and his wife the moon lived on the earth, and the water had never visited their house. When at last the water came, it flowed in and rose higher and higher, filling every room, until the sun and the moon had to climb onto the roof and then up into the sky itself to escape it, and there they have remained ever since.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale from southern Africa tells why the hare has a split lip. The moon sent the hare to carry a message of comfort to humankind, that just as the moon dies and is reborn, so people would die and live again. But the careless hare muddled the message and told people instead that they would die and not return. Furious at the error that brought death's finality to humankind, the moon struck the hare across the mouth, and the hare's lip has been split ever since.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: An African folktale tells of how the leopard got its spots. In one telling the leopard was once a plain, pale creature, until a friend, often the fire or another animal, marked it. The leopard either asked to be painted to be more beautiful, or was branded for some misdeed. In the version where it is a punishment, the leopard had been deceitful, and the marks were set on its coat so that all the other animals would see it coming and never again be fooled by the spotted hunter.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A West African dilemma tale ends not with a moral but with an unanswered question put to the listeners. A father has three sons, and each performs a marvelous deed to save him: one foresaw the danger, one carried the family to safety, one fought off the threat. The storyteller asks which son deserves the inheritance, and the tale stops there. The audience must argue it out among themselves, and the story becomes a tool for teaching judgment, debate, and the weighing of competing claims.

subtopic: African folktales of animals and wisdom
sentence: A folktale from across Africa explains why dogs live with people while their wild cousins remain in the bush. Long ago the dog and the jackal, or the dog and the wolf, set out together one cold night, and the dog followed the scent of woodsmoke to a human campfire and its warmth and scraps of food. The wild cousin would not come near the fire and the noise of people, and so the dog stayed with humankind and the jackal kept to the wilderness, and so it has been ever since.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: The Geatish warrior Beowulf sailed across the sea to the kingdom of the Danes, where the hall of King Hrothgar had been terrorized for twelve years by the monster Grendel. Grendel was a creature of the marshes, descended from the cursed line of Cain, who came each night to the bright hall and devoured the sleeping warriors. Beowulf, hearing of this grief, came to face the monster, and he vowed to fight Grendel without sword or shield, trusting only the grip of his bare hands.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: When Grendel came to the hall of Heorot that night, Beowulf lay waiting. The monster seized one warrior and devoured him, then reached for Beowulf, and found his arm caught in a grip stronger than any he had ever known. Grendel writhed and pulled in terror to escape, but the hero would not let go, and at last the monster tore himself free only by leaving his whole arm and shoulder behind. Mortally wounded, Grendel fled to die in his marsh, and the hall rejoiced at the trophy hung beneath its roof.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: The triumph over Grendel was brief, for the next night Grendel's mother came to avenge her son, a monstrous water-hag who carried off one of Hrothgar's dearest counselors. Beowulf followed her trail to a dark and dreadful mere, and plunged fully armed into its haunted waters. He sank for the better part of a day before reaching the bottom, where the monster dragged him to her cavern, and there, in a hall beneath the lake, the hero fought her for his life.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: In the cavern beneath the mere, Beowulf's own sword failed him, unable to bite the hide of Grendel's mother. The monster bore him down and drew a knife, and only his mail-coat saved his life. Then Beowulf saw upon the wall a great sword forged by giants, too heavy for any ordinary man, and seizing it he struck the monster's neck and killed her. He found Grendel's corpse and cut off its head, and the giant blade melted away in the monster's hot and venomous blood.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: Beowulf returned home laden with honor and gifts, and in time he became king of the Geats, ruling wisely for fifty years. But in his old age a final monster came against his people. A thief disturbed the hoard of a sleeping dragon, stealing a single cup, and the enraged dragon rose from its barrow and burned the countryside, its fiery breath laying waste to the homes and the great hall of the Geats. The aged king resolved to face this last enemy himself.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: Beowulf went to the dragon's barrow with eleven companions, but when the fire-drake came roaring forth, all but one of his warriors fled in terror to the woods. Only the young kinsman Wiglaf stayed at his lord's side. Together the old king and the loyal youth fought the dragon, and Beowulf dealt it a mortal blow, but not before its venomous fangs had pierced his neck. The dragon lay dead and the hoard was won, but the cost of it was the life of the king.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: As Beowulf lay dying, he asked Wiglaf to bring out some of the dragon's treasure so that he might look upon it, and he gave thanks that he had won such a hoard for his people. He commanded that a great barrow be raised on a headland above the sea, a mound that sailors would see from afar and call Beowulf's Barrow. Then the old king died, the last of his line, and the loyal Wiglaf rebuked the warriors who had fled and left their lord to face the dragon nearly alone.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: The Geats built the barrow as Beowulf had commanded, and they placed within it the dragon's hoard, the gold returning to the earth from which it had been dug, useless to the living. Twelve warriors rode around the mound, chanting the praises of their fallen king, lamenting that he had been the gentlest and kindest of men, the most courteous to his people, and the most eager for fame. The poem ends in mourning, the monsters slain but the hero gone and his folk left defenseless.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: The world of Beowulf is one in which monsters press always at the edges of the lighted hall. Grendel comes out of the dark fen, his mother from the haunted mere, the dragon from the ancient barrow. The hall, with its fire and its fellowship and its songs, is a fragile circle of human warmth, and the hero is the one who steps out of that circle into the darkness to hold the monsters back. The poem knows that the holding cannot last forever, and that every hall will fall in its time.

subtopic: Norse heroes Beowulf and the monster tradition
sentence: Grendel was given a name that the old tradition used for the outcast and the kin of monsters, and he was said to descend from Cain, the first murderer, cursed and exiled from the company of humankind. The monsters of the heroic tradition were not random horrors but figures of exile, envy, and the dark that lay outside the bonds of kinship and the gift-giving of the hall. Grendel hated the sound of the harp and the joy of men precisely because he was shut out from it forever.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The ballad of Tam Lin tells of a young man held captive by the Queen of the Fairies, who guards the well of Carterhaugh. The bold Janet, having met and loved him, learns that the fairies pay a tithe to hell every seven years and that Tam Lin fears he will be the next offering. To save him she must catch him as he rides in the fairy procession on Halloween and hold him fast while the fairies transform him in her arms into a newt, a bear, a lion, and a burning brand.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: Thomas the Rhymer, a poet of the Scottish borders, met the Queen of Elfland beneath the Eildon Tree and was carried away with her on a milk-white steed. They rode through rivers of blood and past the three roads, the narrow thorny path of righteousness, the broad road of wickedness, and the bonny road to fair Elfland. Thomas dwelt in the fairy realm for what seemed three days but was seven years, and when he returned he was given a tongue that could not lie and the gift of true prophecy.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The ballad of the wife of Usher's Well tells of a mother whose three sons went to sea and were lost. In her grief she wished a terrible wish, that the wind would never cease until her sons came home to her. One winter night they came, their hats made of the bark of the birch that grew at the gates of paradise, and the mother feasted them and made their beds. But at the crowing of the cock the dead sons had to depart, returning to the grave and bidding farewell to the mother and the fire.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The border ballads were full of the restless dead returning to the living. In the ballad of Sweet William's Ghost, the dead lover comes to his betrothed's window to ask her to release him from his promise of marriage, for he cannot rest in the grave while the vow stands. She begs a kiss, but he warns that his lips are cold clay and a kiss would mean her death. The ballads insisted that an oath bound even beyond the grave, and that the dead and the living owed each other dangerous debts.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The legend of the brownie belonged to the farms and houses of the Scottish lowlands and borders. The brownie was a small, rough, hairy spirit attached to a household, who came out at night to thresh the grain, sweep the floors, and finish the work the family had left undone. The brownie asked nothing but a bowl of cream or fresh bread set out for him. He must never be paid with clothing or thanked too openly, for an offered gift would offend him, and the affronted brownie would depart and never return.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The ballad of the Twa Corbies, the two ravens, is among the bleakest of the border songs. Two carrion crows discuss where they will dine, and one tells of a slain knight lying behind an old turf wall. None knows he lies there, for his hawk, his hound, and his lady have all forsaken him, the lady already gone to a new love. The ravens settle on the feast they will make of him, and the wind blows forever over his white and scattered bones, and no one mourns.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The legend of the kelpie haunted the lochs and rivers of Scotland with a particular dread. In the ballad and folk traditions the water horse was a shape-shifting predator, appearing as a fine gray or black horse to tempt a rider, and especially eager to drown children who climbed playfully onto its lengthening back. Some tales said the kelpie could also take the form of a handsome man, and that a woman who noticed waterweed in her suitor's hair had narrowly escaped a watery death.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The ballad of Sir Patrick Spens tells of a Scottish sea captain commanded by the king to sail in the dead of winter. Sir Patrick read the letter and laughed, then his eyes filled with tears, for he knew the voyage in such a season meant his death. He and his lords set sail, and the storm took them, and the ballad lingers on the Scottish ladies waiting with their fans and their gold combs for husbands who would never come home, for half over to Aberdour it is fifty fathoms deep.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The legend of the each-uisge, the water horse of the Scottish Highlands, made it even more deadly than the lowland kelpie. The each-uisge lived in the sea and the deep lochs, and when it carried a victim into the water, it tore them apart and devoured everything but the liver, which floated to the surface. So feared was the creature that Highlanders were wary of any lone horse or pony found near the water, and would not touch a strange beast that might be the each-uisge wearing a gentle shape.

subtopic: Scottish and English border ballads and legends
sentence: The English legend of Herne the Hunter placed a ghostly figure in the great forest of Windsor, a spectral huntsman wearing the antlers of a stag upon his head. He was said to ride out on stormy nights, leading a phantom hunt of baying hounds, and his appearance was an omen of misfortune for the realm. The legend, like the wider tradition of the Wild Hunt, gathered around the figure of the antlered hunter all the old dread of the forest, the storm, and the powers that moved through the night.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: In the beginning, the Greeks said, there was only Chaos, a yawning void. From it emerged Gaia, the broad-breasted earth, and Tartarus, the deep pit beneath, and Eros, the force of desire. Gaia brought forth Uranus, the starry sky, to cover her on every side, and from the union of earth and sky came the first generations of beings: the twelve Titans, the one-eyed Cyclopes, and the hundred-handed giants, the Hecatoncheires.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: Uranus, the sky father, hated his monstrous children, the Cyclopes and the hundred-handed ones, and he thrust them back into the body of Gaia, the earth, causing her terrible pain. In her anguish Gaia fashioned a great sickle of unbreakable adamant and called on her children to punish their father. Only the youngest and boldest of the Titans, Cronus, took up the weapon, and when Uranus next came down to lie with Gaia, Cronus struck and overthrew his father, ending the reign of the sky.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: Cronus, having overthrown his father Uranus, became the ruler of the cosmos, but he carried his father's dying curse: that he too would be overthrown by his own child. To escape the prophecy, Cronus swallowed each of his children the moment they were born, sealing the infant gods within his own body. His wife Rhea, grieving for her devoured children, resolved that her sixth child would not be lost, and when Zeus was born she hid him away and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: Zeus was raised in secret on the island of Crete, hidden from his father in a cave and nourished by a divine goat. When he came to manhood, he returned to confront Cronus, and with a potion he forced the Titan to vomit up the children he had swallowed: Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon, all emerging fully grown, along with the stone that had been swallowed in Zeus's place. The freed gods rallied to their brother, and the war for the cosmos began.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: The Titanomachy was a war of ten years between the young gods led by Zeus and the older Titans led by Cronus. Neither side could gain the upper hand until Zeus, advised by Gaia, descended into Tartarus and freed the Cyclopes and the hundred-handed giants whom Uranus and Cronus had imprisoned. In gratitude the Cyclopes forged for Zeus his thunderbolts, for Poseidon his trident, and for Hades a helmet of invisibility, and with these weapons the tide of the war turned.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: With the thunderbolts of Zeus and the boulders hurled by the hundred-handed giants, the young gods at last shattered the power of the Titans. Cronus and his defeated allies were cast down into the gloom of Tartarus, sealed behind bronze gates and guarded by the hundred-handed ones. The three brothers then divided the cosmos by lot: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the underworld, while the earth remained common ground, and so the reign of the Olympians began.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: Not all the Titans fought against Zeus, and not all were punished. Prometheus, whose name meant forethought, had foreseen the outcome and sided with the Olympians, and so he kept his freedom for a time. The Titan Atlas, however, had led the enemy forces, and for this Zeus condemned him to a punishment without end: to stand at the western edge of the world and bear the weight of the heavens upon his shoulders forever, keeping sky and earth apart.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: The Titan Prometheus became the great benefactor and the great rebel of Greek myth. He shaped humankind from clay, and when Zeus withheld fire from the mortals, Prometheus stole a spark from the heavens, hidden in the hollow of a fennel stalk, and carried it down to humanity. For this defiance Zeus chained him to a rock in the Caucasus, where an eagle came each day to tear out his liver, which grew whole again each night, an agony renewed without end until a hero finally freed him.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: The reign of Cronus and the Titans was remembered by the Greeks, in a strange double vision, as a lost golden age. They told that under Cronus, before the rule of Zeus, humankind lived without toil or sorrow, the earth yielding its fruit freely, and people grew old gently and died as if falling asleep. The overthrow of the Titans had brought the Olympian order, but it had also, the old stories hinted, ended an age of innocence that could never come again.

subtopic: Greek primordial gods and the Titanomachy
sentence: After the defeat of the Titans, Gaia, the earth, was not content with the rule of her grandson Zeus, and she brought forth one last and most terrible challenger. The monster Typhon rose against the Olympians, a creature vast beyond measure with a hundred dragon-heads and a voice of every kind of sound. The gods fled in terror to Egypt, taking the forms of animals to hide, and Zeus alone stood his ground, and only after a cataclysmic battle did he bury Typhon beneath a mountain and secure his throne.
